"Earlier on in my life, even before 'The Martian,' I wanted to bring back audio-only entertainment."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Hot off the tremendous theatrical success of this year's "Project Hail Mary," adapted from Andy Weir's 2021 novel of the same name, the New York Times bestselling author is rocketing back into deep space with a brand new Audible Original release landing on Nov. 5, 2026, titled "Exoplanet."

Weir ("The Martian") is executive producing this ambitious full-cast audiobook drama with acclaimed author and ace comic writer Benjamin Percy ("Wolverine") for the first in a series of curated sci-fi projects for Amazon's Audible.

The seven-episode sci-fi thriller stars the vocal talents of Anthony Mackie, Ariana DeBose, and John Leguizamo in a wild time-travel space disaster odyssey that also benefits from Lucasfilm’s Skywalker Sound, which provided the show’s immersive acoustic elements.

"One crew. One planet. Three timelines. No one survives alone," states the official synopsis. "When a quantum anomaly tears apart the starship Wild Blue Yonder, each surviving crew member crash-lands in a different era on the same deadly exoplanet—hunted, alone, and running out of time."

Ahead of the audio drama's launch, we sat down with Weir and Percy to find out more about this exciting science fiction adventure.

When Percy was first approached by Audible about this challenging endeavor, it was part of a bake-off situation where he was competing with several other writers, all jockeying for position.

"I think the thing that set me apart is my understanding of how to channel legacy properties," Percy tells Space. "Having written for DC and for Marvel, I can take 'Star Wars' or 'Predator' or Wolverine or Batman and honor that legacy but also put my own unique spin on it.

"When it came to the banner of 'Andy Weir Presents,' my job was to write my best version of an awesome Andy Weir story. So I thought about space disasters, big-hearted hopefulness, quippy humor, and a roller coaster plot, and then I nested into all of that a time-travel story."

Writing an audio drama is unlike the comic work that Percy is known for, but as he explains, it's also quite different from working on conventional shows and movies too.

"If you’re watching TV or film, you’re passive and letting it wash over you. You’re taking in the story as a passenger," notes Percy. "But when you're listening to audio, you're invited in with the dialogue, the narration, the sound cues. You’re invited to fill in the vacancies. As a result of that, you become like a co-author in the experience. I was super excited to jump into this project."

The genesis of "Exoplanet" started with Audible approaching Weir with the basic idea, but what they didn't know was that he had already been thinking about resurrecting great radio dramas of the past.

"Earlier on in my life, even before 'The Martian,' I wanted to bring back audio-only entertainment with full-cast productions and sound effects," shares Weir. "I got into listening to things like 'The Lone Ranger' and 'The Shadow' and, of course, the Basil Rathbone Sherlock Holmes adaptations. Also, 'Zorro' was a radio show, and there were a lot of good westerns.

"At the time, I wasn't yet famous or a writer, but I thought I could do this myself. I could write something, narrate it, throw in some sound effects, and put it up online," Weir recalls. "But then I didn't because I’m really lazy. Then many moons later, Audible comes up to me, and I have an opportunity to participate in that exact thing. I especially like the part where all the hard work is done by Ben. That’s my favorite part."

As Weir points out, he's thankfully not the one wielding the pen this time around, but he did select Percy to be his champion.

"We got a bunch of different story concepts submitted to us from lots of talented authors, and Ben's was the one that stood out head and shoulders above the rest. It’s a really interesting concept," says Weir.

"It's not just trope sci-fi with an evil empire of bad guys and some plucky rebels. Ben came up with a unique story with a unique angle. Audio is quickly becoming a larger and larger medium. Everyone's on the go, and now for the first time in history we all have computers in our pocket capable of storing multiple audiobooks to last us years. It's a great time to revive the old art of radio plays, and I think this is a great way to do it.”

Weir's enthusiasm for the project is clear, and we can't wait to check it out. And we won't have to, because it releases today!

"Exoplanet" is available starting Nov. 5 exclusively from Audible for members of its subscription tiers or as an a la carte option.

One crew. One planet. Three timelines. No one survives alone. A sci-fi thriller executive produced by Andy Weir (#1 bestselling author of Project Hail Mary, The Martian), with an all-star cast led by Anthony Mackie, Ariana DeBose and John Leguizamo.

Exoplanet is free for Audible members, but also available for purchase separately.

Jeff Spry is an award-winning screenwriter and veteran freelance journalist covering TV, movies, video games, books, and comics. His work has appeared at SYFY Wire, Inverse, Collider, Bleeding Cool and elsewhere. Jeff lives in beautiful Bend, Oregon amid the ponderosa pines, classic muscle cars, a crypt of collector horror comics, and two loyal English Setters.

#821. Who are the main candidates for the Aberdeen job?

Steven Pressley, John McGlynn and Steve Clarke have all been mentioned in despatches

Another season, another managerial sacking at Aberdeen.

Stephen Robinson's departure on Monday made it five dismissals since the spring of 2021.

The Northern Irishman followed Stephen Glass, Jim Goodwin, Barry Robson and Jimmy Thelin in making an abrupt exit on the watch of chairman Dave Cormack.

Most of the quintet have lasted less than a year and, although Thelin ended the Dons' 35-year wait to win the Scottish Cup, the general trend has been one of perceived underachievement in Scottish Premiership.

Derek McInnes, now with Rangers after spells at Kilmarnock and Heart of Midlothian, was the last Pittodrie boss to regularly deliver consistent results in the top flight and consequent European qualification.

So who could be next? And what qualities does such a manager require?

'Aberdeen hunt yet another manager after ill-fated Robinson reign'

Aberdeen sack Robinson after league slump

Falkirk add goals and grit to McGlynn's guile on rapid rise

Two names mentioned fairly early on after Robinson's exit were Dundee's Steven Pressley and Falkirk's John McGlynn.

Both have impressed in the Premiership this past 17 months, drawing admirers for style of play and good results.

Falkirk are third in the division, two places above Dundee, and McGlynn's side were sixth last season, again two places higher than Pressley's men.

Former Aberdeen defender Richard Foster said the pair are "the two that stand out for me domestically" and said of Elgin-born Pressley on BBC Radio Scotland's Breakfast: "I know he's got a quiet, laid-back demeanour, but I think in the dressing room, he commands respect.

"The players at Dundee seem to love playing for him.

"He knows the game very well. Having played at Hearts, having played at Celtic, he knows what it's like to be at a huge club."

Former Hearts, Hibernian and Scotland midfielder Michael Stewart has been impressed with McGlynn's track record of signing players.

Speaking on McGlynn on BBC Radio Scotland's Sportsound, Stewart said: "John McGlynn puts the miles in.

"He's up and down the road down south. He's up and around all over Scotland. He knows what the players are that are perhaps not in the eye of many others. He knows them intimately before they arrive at Falkirk.

"So it's no great surprise that his success rate with recruitment is pretty, pretty good.

"I would not be surprised if, whenever one or two of the bigger jobs start coming up... rather than being sort of an outsider, I think he'll be right in the hunt for some of those jobs."

Former Celtic and Hibs midfielder Scott Allan says McGlynn is "very tactically astute" and commented: "I love everything that John McGlynn does. Everybody in Scottish football can respect the job he's done there, the consistency.

"He's one of the most prepared managers, if not the most prepared manager for any sort of set-up that he faces week-to-week and he's shown that.

"It's a fantastic job he's done over the last three or four years. He deserves all the credit that comes his way."

It may seem like a lifetime ago, but it's actually only been five months since Steve Clarke stepped down as Scotland head coach.

The 63-year-old, like McGlynn, has vast coaching experience, including in Scotland after a two-year spell with Kilmarnock.

Clarke oversaw three qualifications to major tournaments with Scotland, ending long waits to appear at the European Championship and World Cup.

As well as managerial stints at West Bromwich Albion and Reading, Clarke has worked at Chelsea, Liverpool and Newcastle United, so little would daunt the former right-back.

Appointing Clarke would be a statement by Aberdeen and the challenge of restoring the club to competitiveness may be a compelling one for the man himself.

However, along with McGlynn, geography may play a part and their candidacy could depend on whether personal circumstances allow a switch to the north east.

Wigan Athletic boss and former Scotland centre-half Gary Caldwell has also been linked with the Pittodrie job. The 44-year-old cut his managerial teeth with the Latics and returned there earlier this year after spells in charge of Chesterfield, Partick Thistle and Exeter City.

Swede Thelin stands out as one of the few overseas managers Aberdeen have had.

Yes, Goodwin and Robinson hail from Ireland and Northern Ireland respectively, but both are very much embedded in Scottish football after spending so much time at various clubs north of the border.

The only other non-Scottish manager to grace the Pittodrie home dugout was the Dane, Ebbe Skovdahl, from 1999-2002.

As such, it is fair to say Aberdeen have not experimented too much with foreign coaches and have tended to go with faces familiar to the Scottish top flight.

With a German, Lutz Pfannenstiel, as the sporting director, Aberdeen look further afield this time?

It has become the vogue in the Premiership of late, with Hearts, Hibs and Motherwell going foreign, with Belgian Wouter Vrancken, Dutchman Marink Reedijk and Swede Alfred Johansson in recent months.

Should Pfannenstiel unearth the next Jens Berthel Askou, formerly of Motherwell, Dons fans will be delighted.

Podcast: What is going wrong at Aberdeen?

https://www.bbc.co.uk/sounds/play/p0pm7gkd

Former Aberdeen defender Stuart Duff is in interim charge of Aberdeen following the departures of Robinson, assistant Brian Kerr and coach Stephen Craigan.

The Dons are second bottom of the Premiership, two points above Kilmarnock.

Unless an appointment is made during the international break, Duff faces taking Aberdeen to face Kilmarnock on 21 November before visiting Rangers three days later, with their next home game being against Dundee on 28 November.

Confidence is low after seven league defeats so far this season, but the tightly-packed middle section of the league means Aberdeen are only a couple of wins off the top six.

#820. Freddie Prinze Jr. & Sarah Michelle Gellar’s Son, 14, Drives Porsche

Freddie Prinze Jr. and Sarah Michelle Gellar's 14-year-old son Rocky shared his latest zooming adventure: getting the chance to race around in a Porsche.

Rocky Prinze is ready to lap the competition.

The 14-year-old son of Freddie Prinze Jr. and Sarah Michelle Gellar has been deep into racing over the past year and took his skills to a new level as he got behind the wheel of a Porsche.

Rocky posted several photos of himself with a gray Porsche coupe to Instagram Nov. 6, sharing a quote by auto founder Ferdinand Porsche reading, "In the beginning I looked around and could not find quite the car I dreamed of. So I decided to build it myself.”

Rocky captioned the monumental moment, "My first time driving one.”

In the pics—shared in a joint post with his dad—the teen posed at the wheel, as well as on top of and next to the fast car.

And his parents have been revving up their support for his racing dreams, with Freddie posting about Rocky’s ambitions in March. The She’s All That star shared a video of his son speeding around a track on Instagram, writing, “Day 1. My son Rocky putting in that work on his dream.”

And it’s been his goal to get fast and furious from a very young age, with Rocky even sharing a snap of a project he did as a little kid in which he said he really likes “to race cars.” He captioned the August Instagram pic, “Living my kindergarten dream.”

Sarah—who also shares daughter Charlotte, 17, with Freddie—encouraged her followers to keep up with her son as he zooms into a new chapter, posting a photo of him on a go-kart and saying, “We know you’ve heard us talk about Rocky racing… but now you can follow his competition journey.”

The Buffy the Vampire Slayer alum previously shared that she and Freddie are doing everything they can to get pumped for their son’s dream of becoming a Formula 1 driver when he’s older.

"How do we foster that for him? I don't know a lot about F1 and racing, so it's like finding those contacts," she told People in March. "And luckily, I worked with someone who's quite a prominent racer—Patrick Dempsey."

For a sweet look at Sarah and Freddie speeding through life with their kids, keep reading.

Driving home the fact that son Rocky looks just like dad Freddie Prinze Jr., Sarah Michelle Gellar shared a photo from a "race weekend with my boys" in October 2026.

The actress celebrated the aspiring F1 driver completing another lap around the sun and turning 14. "I should have known from your speedy delivery, the excitement you would bring," she wrote on Instagram in September 2026. "You have no idea how lucky I feel to watch you chase your dream. You inspire not just me, but everyone around you."

Sarah also paid tribute to her "best friend" and daughter Charlotte, who was born three years and one day prior to her little brother."I’m not sure how you are 17 already," the Buffy the Vampire Slayer star shared on Instagram in September 2026. "You may have been the child that made me a mom, but now you are the person that brings out the best in me. (Not to mention my biggest champion) Thank you… for being you."

Not switching gears, Rocky's mom shared a heartfelt post when he turned 13."Aside from being one of the fastest in the state, you are one of the most polite, kind and funny kids I know," she penned on Instagram in September 2025. "I can’t believe you are a teenager. I love you more than my words can express!!!"

As the sun set on an old year and rose on a new, Sarah, Freddie and the kids enjoyed a trip to Hawaii—with her posting a "vacation dump" in January 2024.

Fans know what this crew did that summer. The I Know What You Did Last Summer costars took their children on a trip to Italy in July 2023.

Sarah's intentions for this adorable throwback? To celebrate Rocky's birthday!"Your laugh is infectious, your jokes are the best and your spirit is … EVERYTHING," the Cruel Intentions alum raved on Instagram in September 2023. "You make every day brighter."

Making a rare red carpet appearance, Charlotte joined her mom at the L.A. screening of Sarah's movie Do Revenge in September 2022.

Scooby-Dooby-Doo, where are you? The Scooby-Doo costars and their children returned to Hawaii to say goodbye to 2021 and hello to 2022.

For Charlotte's birthday in 2021, Sarah reflected on how "this day 12 years ago my greatest life truly began."

And on Rocky's 9th birthday that year, the Ringer celeb looked back at when he was born and his parents' "hearts exploded."

This 2019 photo of Charlotte starting fourth grade and Rocky beginning first is one for the books.

Sarah gave a shout-out to her husband on Father's Day 2016."The greatest part of every day is watching life through my children's eyes," she wrote on Instagram, "so today (and every day) Freddie I thank you."

After Charlotte was cast as baby Simba in a children's production of The Lion King, her mom shared a snap of her using Freddie's binder to study lines."So no matter how hard we have tried (and believe me we have tried) to convince our daughter to find any hobby but performing, she has shown a great love (and talent) for being on the stage," Sarah wrote on Instagram in 2016 before joking, "(wonder where she gets that from?)."

"In my household cooking is family time, time to #unplug and connect," the cookbook author wrote on Instagram in 2015 alongside a photo of her and her little ones. "I treasure these moments."

The first iROSA arrays were deployed in 2021.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Just as NASA is preparing to demonstrate "Max Power" on the ground, two astronauts on a spacewalk have provided the International Space Station (ISS) with the same.

Expedition 75 flight engineers Anil Menon of NASA and Joshua Kutryk of the Canadian Space Agency installed and deployed the eighth and final ISS Roll-Out Solar Array (iROSA) on Thursday (Nov. 5), augmenting the space station's legacy solar array wings to produce as much as 30% more electricity.

"We got it done!" said Menon at the end of the 6-hour-and-59-minute spacewalk. The EVA (extravehicular activity) began at 8:36 a.m. EST and ended at 3:35 p.m. EST (1336 to 2035 GMT).

Repeating many of the same tasks as they did on an Oct. 29 spacewalk that added the penultimate iROSA, Menon and Kutryk worked this time on the starboard side of the station's backbone truss on the 3B power channel. The two retrieved the 750-pound (340 kilograms) iROSA assembly from a temporary stowage platform, carried it to the worksite by way of the Canadarm2 robotic arm and mounted it to its previously assembled bracket kit.

Menon then attached the cables to tie the iROSA into the station's systems but ran into a problem.

"We are seeing half of the expected shunt current that we want," radioed Nichole Stilwell, a NASA astronaut serving as the spacewalk officer in Mission Control. "In this current config, we are not necessarily going to deploy."

To address the issue, the connectors needed to be inspected. Out of safety concerns — given that the arrays generate electricity whenever lit by the sun — the astronauts needed to wait for the space station to enter the shadow of Earth to see what could be done. In the interim, they spent the time cleaning up their worksite and returning the Canadarm2 to its park site as they would have done after the deployment.

Fortunately, they were able to clear the issue.

"We are seeing good shunt currents on the ground, so we are go for deploy," said Stilwell.

After releasing two bolts, Kutryk and Menon watched as the array started to unfurl to its full 63-foot (19 meters) length. No motor was needed; the iROSA, as designed, used only the potential energy stored by its rolled-up carbon composite booms to extend itself. The entire process took about 10 minutes.

"Today marks the completion of not just one solar array but, over 15 years after its development, eight arrays," said Menon at the close of the spacewalk. "These solar arrays are incredible. Half the size of the old ones and bringing 40% more power."

Each of the eight iROSAs and their mounting assemblies were delivered to the space station by SpaceX Dragon cargo spacecraft. Beginning in June 2021, four teams of two astronauts did as was done on Thursday to deploy each array. In addition to Kutryk and Menon's work on the 2A and 3B power channels, the spacewalkers included Shane Kimbrough of NASA and Thomas Pesquet of the European Space Agency for the 2B and 4B channels; Josh Cassada and Frank Rubio, both with NASA, on 3A and 4A in December 2022; and NASA's Steve Bowen and Woody Hoburg on 1A and 1B in June 2023.

The need for the iROSA augmentations was discovered by flight controllers when the space station's eight original arrays began to show degraded power output as they exceeded their 15-year design life. The iROSAs provide the additional electricity needed to support ISS operations through its retirement and controlled deorbit, which are currently scheduled to occur in late 2030.

"Congratulations to you all on your stellar work to finish the last of the roll-out solar arrays and the upgrades to the ISS power system that will take it to the end of its journey," said Stilwell, addressing Menon and Kutryk. "It is fitting that we just surpassed 26 years of constant human presence on the International Space Station, and you all showed us what the best of humanity looks like executing one of the most difficult and dangerous [things] humans do and making it look easy. Congratulations!"

Menon has now logged 33 hours and 30 minutes on four spacewalks, while Kutryk has tailed 14 hours and 10 minutes on two EVAs. Thursday's spacewalk was the 101st U.S. EVA at the International Space Station without a space shuttle being present and the 286th overall in support of ISS assembly, maintenance and upgrades. It was the ninth spacewalk of 2026 and the sixth conducted by the station's 75th resident crew.

Robert Pearlman is a space historian, journalist and the founder and editor of collectSPACE.com, a daily news publication and community devoted to space history with a particular focus on how and where space exploration intersects with pop culture. Pearlman is also a contributing writer for Space.com and co-author of "Space Stations: The Art, Science, and Reality of Working in Space” published by Smithsonian Books in 2018.In 2009, he was inducted into the U.S. Space Camp Hall of Fame in Huntsville, Alabama. In 2021, he was honored by the American Astronautical Society with the Ordway Award for Sustained Excellence in Spaceflight History. In 2023, the National Space Club Florida Committee recognized Pearlman with the Kolcum News and Communications Award for excellence in telling the space story along the Space Coast and throughout the world.

#817. Dortmund fans' group criticises Nmecha celebration

Felix Nmecha joined Borussia Dortmund from Wolfsburg in 2023

A Christian group for footballers says it wants to "demonstrate love and respect towards everyone" following criticism from Borussia Dortmund fans of midfielder Felix Nmecha's goal celebration.

A supporters' group said it objected to Nmecha's goal celebration because it referenced a campaign by Ballers in God called 'The King's Return'.

The supporters' group said, external the campaign discriminates against homosexuality and transgender people, paints abortion as "Satan's plan" and is at odds with Dortmund's values of tolerance and respecting diversity.

To celebrate his two goals in the 2-1 win over Elversberg on Saturday, Nmecha pointed to the sky and mimed taking a crown off his head and placing it on the ground.

He said there were "misunderstandings" over his celebration and that it was "not intended to promote myself or any organisation".

Citing a recent investigation by German broadcaster ARD, the fans' group said "extremely conservative positions against homosexuality and transgender identity are advocated" by the campaign.

Ballers in God, external was created by former Crystal Palace and Tottenham midfielder John Bostock.

The organisation promotes Christian beliefs and has high-profile followers such as England's Marc Guehi and Bukayo Saka and former Brazil forward Kaka.

In response to the supporters' group's claims, Ballers in God said: "We are encouraged by player-led movements such as The King's Return, where footballers themselves take the initiative to express their faith in Jesus.

"Our desire is not only to share our hope, but to demonstrate love and respect towards everyone, including those who do not share our beliefs.

"Our focus has always been, and will always be, to point people to Jesus with grace and love."

Nmecha said: "My message has never been about promoting intolerance, discrimination, or hate in any form."

Last year the Premier League withdrew from the Rainbow Laces campaign and ended its partnership with LGBTQ+ charity Stonewall.

In 2024 then Ipswich captain Sam Morsy, a Muslim, said he did not wear a rainbow armband because of his "religious beliefs".

Guehi wrote "I [heart] Jesus" on his rainbow armband when he captained Palace.

#816. Sofia Franklyn Calls Out Alex Cooper & Matt Kaplan for Memoir Comments

Alex Cooper and Matt Kaplan's comments about Sofia Franklyn's memoir Daddy Issues have caused the former Call Her Daddy podcaster to wonder "how dirty" her ex-coworker will go.

That's how former Call Her Daddy co-host Sofia Franklyn—whose public falling out with Alex Cooper led to her split from the podcast in 2020—felt until she learned Cooper and her husband Matt Kaplan have allegedly taken issue with her memoir behind closed doors.

"I have heard that some people mentioned in the book, some main characters in my book, are working very hard to discredit this story," Franklyn revealed on The Bossticks podcast Nov. 9. "I thought I was bulletproof, and then I started to think how dirty are they gonna play?"

And the 34-year-old wasn't afraid to call out her former creative collaborator—who runs the Unwell podcast network with Kaplan—by name.

As Franklyn quipped, "I'm talking about Alex and Matt, hi. And if you're listening, hi."

The podcaster said that hearing what Cooper and Kaplan allegedly said about Daddy Issues in private has made her question what the pair might do in public to shut down her side of the narrative.

"Are they gonna go after people I love?" Franklyn questioned. "That, I do not like. If my family, my husband, becomes collateral, that actually scares me."

And the concerns have put a dent in Franklyn's armor as she rolls out her book, she said.

"I thought I was gonna go into this process being like, two middle fingers in the air," she continued, conceding, "We'll see how that plays out."

Cooper has previously shared why she continued CHD under Barstool Sports while Franklyn wanted to find a new network in her Hulu docuseries Call Her Alex, stating, "Sofia didn't want to take the deal, but I did, so I stayed. I realized the 'Daddy Gang' was bigger than both of us."

E! News has reached out to Cooper's reps for comment regarding Franklyn's allegations but has not yet heard back.

Still, Franklyn is hopeful that fans of Call Her Daddy who discounted her perspective six years ago may have a different opinion this time around.

In the author's words, "It's going to be a lot harder to discredit me now because the audience is smarter now," adding that she's witnessed online how "people are slightly more aware of how media PR headlines work."

Since adding multiple podcasts under the Unwell umbrella, Cooper has been accused of "sick and twisted" behavior by former employee Alix Earle. The bad blood over Earle's canceled podcast Hot Mess became public when the Florida influencer cosigned a TikTok claiming her ex-boss' success came from her "ambulance chaser" approach with vulnerable podcast guests.

In response to engaging with the video, Cooper invited Earle to speak openly about her allegations instead of "passive aggressive reposts" in her own TikTok.

As such, Franklyn believes she knows how Cooper might use her media savvy to retaliate amid her book's release.

"If someone's playing really gnarly, they are reaching out to your college roommates, people you worked with, people that you've had two, maybe one experience with," she explained, "and they're asking them, 'What can you tell me about this person?' And then I don't know exactly how they'll try to flip it."

And with that in mind, Franklyn made sure to be brutally honest when recounting her life story.

Even if the truth is "embarrassing," "shameful" or "horrible" to look back on, she said, "I'm going to be real as f--k."

And the memorable friendship breakup isn't the only celebrity feud still blazing. Read on for more...

Sex and the City costars Kim and SJP had dodged feud rumors for years. But they were reignited after Kim decided not to return for a third movie and made comments about her costar that raised eyebrows.

"What was your reaction to Kim Cattrall telling Piers Morgan that you were never friends just colleagues?" Andy Cohen asked SJP on a September 2017 episode of Watch What Happens Live.

As she explained, "Just...heartbroken. I mean that whole week, you and I spoke about it because I was just...I don't know I found it really upsetting because that's, you know, that's not the way I recall our experience."

"So...it's sad but I'm kind of...I don't know, I always think that what ties us together is this singular experience is the thing," she contined. "It was a professional experience but it became personal because it was years and years of our lives. So I'm hoping that that sort of eclipses anything that's been recently spoken. That many years spent doing something so special that people had a connection with is such a privileged."

And though they didn't film scenes together, Kim did make a small appearance on And Just Like That.

During a 2022 TikTok challenge, JoJo Siwa described Candace Cameron Bure as the "rudest" celebrity, later explaining that she felt snubbed when Bure once refused to take a picture with her on a red carpet. Shortly after the dig, however, the Full House alum apologized: "I kind of broke your 11-year-old heart. I didn't take a picture with you. Ugh! I feel crummy, I feel—JoJo, I'm so sorry."

The two made amends. But months later, Candace was asked if she expects the Great American Family network, of which she serves as chief creative officer, to feature same-sex couples as leads in holiday movies. She said no, adding, "I think that Great American Family will keep traditional marriage at the core."

JoJo, who came out as a member of the LGBTQ+ community in 2021, wrote on Instagram that the actress' comment is "rude and hurtful to a whole community of people."

In August 2022, Cassadee and Maren traded harsh words with Brittany, wife of fellow country star Jason Aldean, after she shared an Instagram Reel of herself applying makeup on Aug. 23, writing, "I'd really like to thank my parents for not changing my gender when I went through my tomboy phase. I love this girly life."

Bobby (pictured second from left) addressed rumors of a falling out with Tan (middle) in January 2024, two months after he announced his exit from Queer Eye after eight seasons.

"I want people to know that Tan and I—we will be fine," he told Vanity Fair. "There was a situation, and that's between Tan and I, and it has nothing to do with the show. It was something personal that had been brewing—and nothing romantic, just to clarify that."

In March 2024, Tan responded to allegations that he had campaigned to replace Bobby on Queer Eye with his friend Jeremiah Brent.

"Netflix and the production companies did a full-on casting. I didn't put my friend up for the job. They ended up getting it because they were the best person for the job," he said on Instagram. "But I didn't get them hired by getting rid of somebody else."

In September 2023, while playing a game called Stir the Pot with her daughter Kelly Osbourne on E! News, Sharon said the That '70s Show alum was the rudest celebrity she had ever met, branding him, a "rude, rude, rude, rude little boy" and a "dastardly little thing."

He did not respond to her remarks publicly.

Five years prior, Sharon told Larry King that when Ashton appeared on The Talk in 2014, he had an "attitude" after she got his name wrong.

"He goes, 'What are you, what have you done in this industry?'" she recalled. "And I was like, 'Kid, don't start with me, because I'm gonna eat you up and s--t you out.' So I was just like, 'You don't know what you're dealing with, kid.'"

Back in June 2021, Courtney Love accused Olivia Rodrigo of copying her band Hole's album cover for a promotional photo without giving credit. Olivia responded, "Love u and live through this sooooo much." Courtney then replied, "Olivia - you're welcome. My favorite florist is in Notting Hill, London! Dm me for deets! I look forward to reading your note [winking face emoji]."

During a 2019 appearance on Watch What Happens Live, the Happy Days actor was asked why he didn't get along with the Forrest Gump star on the set of the 1989 flick Turner & Hooch.

"I was directing that movie for 13 days," Winkler recalled, "and then I was called into [producer] Jeff Katzenberg's office and he said, 'You have everything with you? Go home.'"

He did, however, seem to get along with Hanks' four-legged costar, quipping, "Love that dog."

Winkler later denied speculation that he still had beef with the Oscar winner, telling TMZ in 2020, "I don't have a feud with Tom Hanks."

Fans of The Hills will remember that iconic line, delivered by Lauren on the season three premiere. Their feud began when Heidi started dating her now-husband Spencer Pratt, and hit its peak when Lauren accused Heidi and Spencer of starting a rumor that she had made a sex tape with then-boyfriend Jason Wahler.

The costars reignited their ongoing feud in 2017 when Tyrese publicly called out Dwayne on Instagram after the Fast and Furious 9 release date was pushed back to April 2020. That same day, it was announced that a Fast and Furious spinoff starring Dwayne and Jason Statham would hit theaters in 2019. The following month, Tyrese threatened to quit Fast 9 if Dwayne was in the movie.

Tyrese then opened up about the feud, telling Van Lathan on The Red Pill podcast, "I have yet to talk to The Rock to this day, and we will have a conversation." He shared that he did have a chat with the former wrestler's producing partner, but not the actor himself.

"I found myself being the messenger on behalf of various people associated to the franchise, but stupid me was the only one who went public about those feelings, which is my own fault," Tyrese said. "It's not professional, it's not cool."

Taylor and Katy had been in a feud for years, their rift even allegedly inspiring Taylor's song "Bad Blood." The drama, which reportedly started over a backup dancer and competing tours, came to an end after Perry sent Taylor a literal olive branch before her Reputation Tour kickoff.

"So I just got to my dressing room and found this actual olive branch," Taylor said in an Instagram video. "This mean so much."

Taylor captioned the video, "Thank you Katy."

The iconic singers have been feuding since 2004. While accepting the Classic Songwriter Award at the Q Awards that year, Elton said to attendees, "Madonna, best f--king live act? F--k off! Since when has lip-syncing been live? Sorry about that, but I think everyone who lip-syncs in public on stage, when you pay like 75 quid to see them, should be shot."

The former Grey's Anatomy star sparked a feud with the series creator in 2008 when she removed her name from the Emmy Awards consideration. The actress stated that her reason for the move was because she wasn't "given the material to warrant a nomination."

Shonda later opened up about Katherine's decision during an interview with Oprah Winfrey on Oprah's Next Chapter in 2012. "On some level it stung and on some level I was not surprised," she said. "When people show you who they are, believe them. I carry that [mantra] with me a lot. It has served me well."

It was the New York Fashion Week fight heard 'round the world when Nicki and Cardi got into a heated altercation at the Harper's Bazaar Icon party. The following month, Cardi opened up about the catalyst for the fight with Nicki.

"For a while now she's been taking a lot of shots at me," Cardi said in W magazine's Art Issue. "I spoke to her twice before, and we came to an understanding. But she kept it going."

The real spark of the fight came when Cardi saw that Nicki had allegedly liked and then unliked a tweet about Cardi's parenting skills, which Nicki has denied.

"I was going to make millions off my Bruno Mars tour, and I sacrificed that to stay with my daughter," Cardi continued. "I love my daughter. I'm a good-ass f--king mom. So for somebody that don't have a child to like that comment? So many people want to say that party wasn't the time or the place, but I'm not going to catch another artist in the grocery store or down the block."

Tension between Kanye and Taylor first started in 2009, when the "Stronger" rapper took the stage during her acceptance speech at the MTV Video Music Awards. Years later, the two would make up and even become friends, but that came to an end in 2016 after the release of his song "Famous," in which he name-checks the "End Game" singer.

In February 2025, one day before the Grammys, Kanye updated his Instagram to follow only Taylor. He added no further comment, and his fellow musician did not respond publicly to the move.

Mariah and J.Lo's supposed feud started when the Queen of Christmas was asked to give her opinion on several singers during a 2003 German TV interview. When asked her opinion on Jennifer, she replied, "I don't know her."

#814. How microbes can secure the critical minerals the world needs

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Gerhard Schenk is a professor and senior research leader at the School of Chemistry and Molecular Biosciences and the Biosustainability Hub, University of Queensland, Brisbane, Australia.

Paul Evans is a research fellow at the School of Chemistry and Molecular Biosciences and the Australian Centre for Ecogenomics, University of Queensland, Brisbane, Australia.

Torben V. Borchert is the scientific director of biomanufacturing at the Novo Nordisk Foundation, Copenhagen, Denmark.

Alan Tordoir is the director of new mining technology at Mining3, Basel, Switzerland.

Susan T. L. Harrison is a professor in bioprocess engineering and deputy vice-chancellor of research and innovation at the University of Queensland, Brisbane, Australia.

Copper compounds (blue) can be extracted from solution using microorganisms — a process known as bioleaching. Credit: Dirk Wiersma/Science Photo Library

The clean-energy transition is creating a paradox. To expand renewable-energy technologies, electrify transport and build infrastructure for artificial intelligence, society must extract unprecedented quantities of minerals. Demand for many of these ‘critical minerals’ is projected to increase several-fold over the coming decades1. Yet, the technologies used to obtain them remain rooted in an old model through which single metals are extracted from virgin ore2.

The consequences are increasingly apparent (see ‘Critical-mineral supply under pressure’). As deposits of high-grade ores decline, larger quantities of rock must be mined and processed to produce the same amount of metal3. That requires more energy and water. Mining accounts for around 1.7% of global energy consumption and this number is projected to rise by up to eight-fold by 20604. Many critical-mineral projects operate in regions facing high water stress, such as arid parts of Africa and Latin America1.

Sources: Top to bottom: Ref. 3; ref. 3; ref. 6 and go.nature.com/4nzbbnx

Mining waste is growing, too. Already, hundreds of billions of tonnes of mine tailings are stored globally. Projections suggest that by 2050, up to two trillion tonnes of extra waste rock and tailings will have accumulated3,5.

Meanwhile, society is producing vast quantities of metal-rich waste that remain a mostly untapped secondary source of metals. In 2022, 62 million tonnes of electronic waste (e-waste) was produced globally — almost 8 kilograms for every person on the planet — and only around 22% of that was formally collected and recycled6.

How to widen access to the critical minerals that the world needs

How to widen access to the critical minerals that the world needs

Many discarded electronics contain valuable metals, including gold, palladium and rare-earth elements — in concentrations that can exceed those found in primary ores. However, recovering these metals remains technically challenging and is often economically unattractive using conventional approaches.

Retrieval of metals and increasing metal circularity should be seen as a strategic capability to offset the growth of metal extraction from virgin ores. Nations that can efficiently recover critical minerals from waste streams, mine residues and low-grade resources will be less exposed to geopolitical disruptions and supply-chain shocks7.

Biology offers a powerful route forwards. Although biomining — which uses microorganisms to extract metals — was once considered a niche approach, it has evolved. Driven by advances in microbial ecology, synthetic biology, structural biology, protein engineering and machine learning, the scientific foundations for a new generation of mineral biotechnologies are emerging at speed8,9. These methods offer potential levels of selectivity for extracting and recovering certain metals that are often difficult to achieve through conventional hydrometallurgical processes.

But, scientific progress alone will not transform mineral supply chains. The main obstacle is no longer a shortage of ideas. It is a lack of pathways from scientific discovery to industrial deployment. Here we outline how to develop those pathways, drawing on discussions at the International Workshop on Biomining of Critical Minerals and Elements, which was sponsored by the Novo Nordisk Foundation and held in Sitges, Spain, in September last year.

Biotechnologies have demonstrated their industrial potential for decades. Bioleaching and biooxidation processes are already established for recovering copper, nickel, gold and cobalt from ores10. They involve irrigating heaps of crushed ore or treating ground mineral powders with specialist microbes that generate chemicals, such as acids or modifiers of reduction–oxidation reactions, that selectively dissolve either target metals or other minerals found with them.

Advances in synthetic biology have expanded the range of potential applications. For example, engineered microbial systems can be designed to dissolve metals more effectively. Biomolecules (such as the protein lanmodulin) can separate rare-earth elements with yields of 99.9% in one step under conditions that are simpler than conventional techniques, using aqueous solutions rather than organic solvents8,11. AI-assisted protein design is further accelerating the discovery of macromolecules designed to selectively recognize, bind to and separate target metals from complex solutions of several elements9.

How the rush for critical minerals is neglecting human needs

How the rush for critical minerals is neglecting human needs

Collectively, these developments suggest that biotechnology could become an important component of future critical-mineral supply chains. However, many promising approaches never progress beyond being validated in the laboratory. They often stall between proof-of-concept studies and commercial demonstration, a challenge familiar throughout industrial biotechnology. Even promising technologies often struggle to attract the capital, infrastructure and industrial partnerships needed to scale them up12,13.

Barriers must be overcome. Although a few bioprocessing pilot projects exist, their capacity is insufficient to evaluate technologies across the diverse types of ore, feedstock and process conditions encountered in practice. Investors are reluctant to finance first-of-a-kind projects when it is uncertain how well they will perform in the real world.

Regulatory frameworks for emerging biomining technologies are also inadequate. They often vary across biotechnology, environmental and mining sectors and between jurisdictions. Developers might need to navigate several regulatory authorities and approval pathways, creating uncertainty and delays as technologies advance.

Electronic waste can contain higher concentrations of key metals than are found in natural ores.Credit: Martin Bernetti/AFP via Getty

In the European Union, for example, the use of genetically modified microorganisms and their environmental applications are subject to distinct regulatory frameworks. Genetically modified microorganisms are allowed to be used in contained systems, whereas those used for field applications generally rely on naturally occurring or adapted microbial strains. The United States uses a coordinated multi-agency approach, involving the Environmental Protection Agency, the Food and Drug Administration and the US Department of Agriculture.

Valuable technical knowledge (on protein engineering, mineral characterization, hydrometallurgy and economic modelling, for instance) remains dispersed across disciplines, institutions and jurisdictions. This makes it difficult to generate the necessary evidence base — including long-term continuous operating data, metrics for tracking chemical cycles and validated economic assessments — to support large-scale adoption of such technologies.

The result is a growing mismatch. Scientific advances in mineral biotechnology are accelerating, yet the mechanisms needed to deploy them are not keeping pace. Although billions of dollars are being invested to secure future supply chains for critical minerals, comparatively little attention has been devoted to building the innovation systems required to commercialize biological solutions.

If biotechnology is to contribute meaningfully to critical-mineral security, environmental sustainability and circularity of resource use, then governments, industry, development banks and philanthropic funders must move beyond supporting research alone. They must invest in the institutions that enable translation of these new technologies as well.

Countries should establish shared pilot and demonstration facilities dedicated to mineral biotechnology. Individual companies often cannot justify the risks associated with developing specialized infrastructure for technologies that remain commercially unproven. Shared facilities can help to overcome this barrier by allowing several organizations to evaluate biological processes using realistic feedstocks under industrially relevant conditions. These facilities can support both pre-commercial and competitive studies. Similar approaches have been implemented successfully in synthetic biology and bio-refining, advanced manufacturing and in the clean-energy and semiconductor sectors.

The dark side of green technology: what do electric vehicles really cost?

The dark side of green technology: what do electric vehicles really cost?

For the mineral sector, such facilities should be located near relevant resource and waste streams, including mining districts, e-waste recycling hubs and sites affected by acid mine drainage or metal-laden urban waste waters. They should have connections to universities, research labs and a skilled workforce.

Access to research and engineering expertise would enable rapid iteration, troubleshooting and integration of mineral biotechnologies with established processes. Such sites would extend beyond technology testing to generate the operational, environmental and economic data needed to inform investment decisions, regulatory approvals and commercial deployment.

Initiatives in other sectors illustrates the value of such infrastructure. In Sweden, for instance, publicly funded pilot and demonstration facilities have been set up to test processes for biochemically converting biomass under realistic conditions14.

A 4.1-billion-year-old meteorite discovered in the Sahara Desert offers a rare glimpse into Mars' early history.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A rose-colored rock discovered in the Sahara Desert may hold some clues to Mars' ancient geological history.

The meteorite, named Teghaza 001 after the salt plain in Mali where it was discovered in 2022, weighs roughly 1.8 pounds (800 grams) and formed more than 4.1 billion years ago. Blasted off Mars by an impact before eventually landing on Earth, it is one of the three oldest Martian meteorites ever found. The extraordinary age and unusual mineral composition of Teghaza 001 offer a rare glimpse into the formation of Mars' early crust and how volcanic materials may have been altered by water, according to a statement from NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California.

"It was only after we started looking closely that we realized this meteorite is really unique,” research leader Yang Liu of NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California said in the statement. "One of the paper’s reviewers called it a Rosetta Stone for Mars."

Unlike many Martian meteorites, Teghaza 001 contains a distinctive combination of igneous minerals and textures that preserve evidence of its complex history. Its mineral composition resembles materials observed in Mars' southern highlands by NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter.

Although researchers can’t pinpoint exactly where the meteorite originated on Mars, they have identified 13 potential locations on the planet where it may have formed.

"This is really our first piece of Martian crust from a part of Mars we’ve never had a sample of before," team member Lee Saper, NASA’s Ames Research Center in Silicon Valley, said. "It records interactions of water and rock and maybe even an imprint of the Martian atmosphere as it was losing water."The meteorite was initially identified as Martian based on its oxygen isotopes. To determine its age, scientists then examined tiny zircon crystals embedded in the rock. Using a specialized rubidium-strontium dating technique, researchers analyzed individual mineral grains on its surface, preserving it for future analysis.

The results revealed that Teghaza 001 was altered by water around 4.1 billion years ago, suggesting the rock itself formed even earlier. The mineral and chemical evidence points to a dynamic water cycle on ancient Mars, when liquid water interacted with the planet's crust and potentially left traces of its atmosphere as it gradually lost water.

Scientists believe further analysis of Teghaza 001 could reveal more about how water shaped the Martian surface and influenced the planet's evolution. The study also marks the first time researchers have used rubidium-strontium dating to analyze an ancient Martian meteorite, opening the door for the technique to be applied to other samples in the future.

"We've only scratched the surface," Liu concluded.

Their findings were published on Thursday (Oct. 29) in the journal Science. A separate study examining the meteorite's water content was published on June 10 in the journal Science Advances, offering additional insight into early Mars.

#812. Wenger considers standing against Infantino

Arsene Wenger (left) joined Fifa as chief of global football development in 2019

Former Arsenal manager Arsene Wenger is considering standing against Gianni Infantino as a candidate in Fifa's presidential election.

For weeks, senior figures in European football have been hoping the Frenchman would run for the job, and he is now giving it serious thought.

Wenger is 77, leading to questions over whether he could provide long-term leadership for the sport.

But some of his supporters have told BBC Sport that they would be happy for him to win the election, then stand down before serving a full four-year term.

Infantino's position was plunged into crisis by a backlash caused by his failed plan to sell commercial stakes in the World Cup to private investors.

But he retains support in South America, Africa and Asia, and recently insisted he has the backing of the "vast, vast majority" of world football.

Infantino laughs off resignation questions

However, that support could be tested if Wenger stands.

Fifa's head of global development would have the backing of Uefa, which has spearheaded opposition to Infantino, and he has credibility throughout the footballing world.

Sources close to Wenger say he is yet to decide whether to stand, and they still believe Infantino is favourite to win a fourth and final term in next year's election.

The deadline for candidates to confirm they are standing against Infantino for the election in March is 18 November.

Former Tottenham defender Ramon Vega was the first person to put his name forward in October.

Japan Football Association honorary president Kozo Tashima has also announced his intention to stand.

This month Fifa said "key documents" relating to Infantino's plan to sell stakes in the World Cup would be made available to members of its council, but they will have to travel to its Zurich base, and access will be under "strict protocols".

Last month Uefa gave football's world governing body until 2 November to release details about the controversial Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal, and to answer questions relating to its decision-making.

That followed a council meeting at which Infantino apologised for the abandoned sell-off plot but failed to explain how the proposal was devised, asking that questions be submitted in writing.

Amid the fallout over FFE, Wenger, who has traditionally been loyal to Infantino, distanced himself from the aborted plot.

"I was not involved in this strategic plan and first became aware of the project through media reports," Wenger said at the time.

"The decision to withdraw the project was absolutely necessary and beyond question, because I firmly believe in an independent Fifa that serves our game with commitment, transparency and integrity."

Wenger has caused controversy at times in his Fifa role, notably for proposals such as biennial World Cups and a "daylight" offside law.

But he also has a global profile, including in Africa, where Infantino recently received a major re-election boost when receiving the backing of all 54 member national associations after promising an increase in funding.

Known as a champion of African players when in charge at Arsenal, Wenger's support of an expanded 48-team World Cup in order to drive development in countries beyond the game's traditional powers has been well received in the continent.

#811. How Germany's greatest goalscorer is guiding the next generation

Miroslav Klose's FC Nuremberg side sit second in the 2. Bundesliga

It is no surprise Miroslav Klose recognises the value of a true goalscorer.

He is, after all, Germany's all-time leading marksman and until this summer had netted more than any other player in men's World Cup history. Even now, only Kylian Mbappe and Lionel Messi can top his 16 across four tournaments.

But of the more than 300 goals Klose scored in a career that began in Germany's amateur leagues and spanned Kaiserslautern, Werder Bremen, Bayern Munich and Lazio, he reckons all but two came inside the penalty area.

"Thankfully, we've moved away a little from the idea of the false nine or having a second striker playing around the main striker, with everyone coming towards the ball," explains the FC Nuremberg boss.

"For me, the most important thing is that you need someone who is there to score goals. You need someone in the box because that's where you're closest to the goal. That's why I'm a big believer in practising the final ball, whether it's a cross, a shot or something else.

"That's crucial. How do you create that final ball? When you develop automatisms and players get to know each other better, that's when you see harmony on the pitch.

"It can make things look effortless, but it involves a huge amount of work. A lot of work in training and attention to detail, making sure the players communicate with each other and understand their team-mates' strengths and weaknesses."

That focus on detail stems from Klose's diligence during his playing days. He would study opponents' movement, analyse a goalkeeper's position and shape when facing certain shots - do they make themselves big? Are their hands high or low?

"When goals are scored, the whole team deserves credit," adds the 48-year-old, who was as selfless as he was ruthless. "But you still need someone who has that ability in their feet or in their head to put the ball in the net."

Klose won the World Cup with Germany in 2014, after losing the 2002 final to Brazil

Klose was 36 when he won the World Cup with Germany in 2014 - surpassing Ronaldo's goal record in a 7-1 semi-final thrashing of hosts Brazil.

It was the culmination of a career built on hard work after a series of near-misses - something that may offer solace to Harry Kane and England that a major tournament triumph remains possible.

Born in communist Poland, Klose's father Josef - also a footballer, most notably for Auxerre - moved the family to West Germany when his son was eight.

He was never in a big academy, playing in the lower leagues while training as a carpenter before eventually joining Kaiserslautern.

Klose, like Kane, was in his early 20s by the time he established himself in top-flight football, but just two years after his Bundesliga debut was starting a World Cup final defeat by Brazil.

The striker, 38 when he hung up his goalscoring boots, admires the way Kane has evolved as he has matured, using him as an example to his own young prospects.

"You could always see his quality, and he's worked incredibly hard to get where he is," says Klose of the Ballon d'Or winner.

"He's also a great role model for me, particularly because he has stayed in Germany. I often tell my players that they should look at someone like him as an example.

"Young players can't yet have the instinct and experience he has developed, but that's where it starts - thinking about what you can and can't do as a footballer. You have to keep learning. That's the crucial thing for me.

"If you understand that you train to become better, then in five years' time you'll naturally be a different player. But if you think everything will happen automatically just because 10 people around you tell you that you're a fantastic player, I don't think you'll continue to develop."

Klose's Nuremberg have the youngest average age in the 2. Bundesliga

Klose has a knack for working with young talent, previously coaching Bayern Munich's under-17s. His Nuremberg side are the youngest in the German second tier with an average age of 23.3 years, according to Transfermarkt.

"You need that balance and a certain core of experienced players," he explains. "But we're very brave in that respect. Over the three years I've been here, we've made progress in how we assess young players and in the conversations we have about them.

"How do we rate them? How far along are they? What do they need to work on to take the next step? Is it perhaps more about their physical development? Because from a footballing perspective, we're already producing some really good players."

Klose's coaching journey began with the national team before he joined Bayern, briefly becoming Hansi Flick's assistant, and then took his first managerial role at Rheindorf Altach in Austria.

He joined Nuremberg, historically one of Germany's most successful clubs, in 2024 and steered them to 10th and eighth-placed finishes.

This season they sit second, behind Hertha BSC, and are the league's joint-top scorers, with eyes on a return to the Bundesliga for the first time since 2019.

"When I first arrived, I spoke to the youth coaches about the club's DNA and its coaching philosophy, and what they focus on," adds Klose.

"There was already a lot of common ground. We suggested trying certain things because we wanted to do a little more in particular areas, and they were open to that.

"That's important. We benefit from this because our young players are getting opportunities in the first team, and everyone is paying attention to their development.

"But that journey starts with the youth coaches. I know how important it is to take those steps. We're benefiting from that now because we have access to so many young talents.

"As a coaching team, we're brave enough to give them opportunities when we see that they can compete at this level. That's the first step."

Among the 11 to play the most minutes for Klose's side this season, seven are 22 years old or under, including top scorer Mohamed Ali Zoma, already capped by Italy.

"Of course, everyone gets a lot of praise, as is currently the case with Marc Kornwachs," says Klose of a 17-year-old midfielder also catching the eye.

"But his journey isn't over yet. Now it's about helping him become more consistent and establishing himself, while continuing to develop his game and take further steps forward.

"These players are so talented that we have absolutely no hesitation in giving them opportunities, regardless of the scoreline."

Klose was still playing fifth-tier amateur football aged 20 before becoming the World Cup's all-time top goalscorer in 2014

Klose also understands his managerial career is still young - mirroring the humble nature that earned him fair play awards in Germany and Italy.

"I'm very comfortable with the steps I've taken, even though it involves a huge amount of work," he says about his progress. "You learn something every day.

"I've said that I'm already a much better manager than I was three years ago. That's perfectly normal, and you have to embrace it. I've always been willing and eager to learn, and I've always been a hard worker. That isn't going to change."

So what does a Miroslav Klose team look like?

"Personally, as a player, I always liked having the ball for long periods, and that hasn't changed," he explains.

"When you have the ball, you have a certain level of dominance. I know you also have to be very adaptable in terms of possession, and that's something we are. We constantly show the players different ways of playing out of situations.

"It's great to see how they develop and to be able to support individual players along the way. That's exactly the approach I like to take as a manager."

#807. Wales call up MK Dons' Collins as Moore withdraws

Aaron Collins (right) has seven goals in the past three games for MK Dons and is the EFL's joint-top goalscorer

Wales have called up uncapped MK Dons striker Aaron Collins for this month's Nations League matches following Wrexham frontman Kieffer Moore's withdrawal due to injury.

Moore, 34, left the field during Wrexham's 1-1 Championship draw with Wolves on Saturday.

Wales have not specified what kind of injury the 57-cap forward has sustained.

He is replaced in the Wales squad by Collins, who has scored 17 goals in 16 games across all competitions for League One side Dons this season, including four goals in a game against Doncaster last month.

The 29-year-old former Newport County player joins Craig Bellamy's squad for concluding Group A4 games in Norway and at home to Portugal.

Newport-born Collins has played for 10 different - mainly lower league - clubs since leaving Rodney Parade for Wolverhampton Wanderers in 2016.

Wales, who are looking to preserve their place in the Nations League's top tier, face Norway in Oslo on Saturday before finishing their campaign at home against Portugal next Tuesday.

Wales are third in Group A4, with their only win from four matches so far coming against World Cup quarter-finalists Norway in Cardiff last month.

Bellamy is without midfielder Jordan James but has influential Leeds pair Harry Wilson and Joe Rodon back, along with Cardiff playmaker Rubin Colwill.

Live on BBC iPlayer, BBC Two Wales, BBC Sounds, BBC Radio Wales, Radio Cymru and 5 Live Sports Extra, BBC Sport website and app, plus live text commentary.

Bellamy's side could still finish in second, third or fourth place.

A top-two spot would take Wales to the Nations League quarter-finals in March 2027.

Finishing third would mean a relegation play-off against a League B team in March, while finishing bottom of the group would result in either a relegation play-off or direct relegation, depending on the ranking with other League A groups.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

NASA will host a first-of-its-kind air show and aerospace expo on Florida's Space Coast this weekend.

The show, called Max Power, will take place Saturday and Sunday (Nov. 7 and Nov. 8) at and around NASA's Kennedy Space Center (KSC). That name should be familiar to "Simpsons" fans, by the way: Max Power is an alias that Homer uses in the 13th episode of the show's 10th season. (He got it off a hair dryer.)

There will be a lot to see at NASA's event, so you should consider dropping by if you're on the Space Coast this weekend. (Tickets are required; you can buy them here.) Here are a few of the highlights.

NASA will also hold a livestreamed press conference on Saturday at 5 p.m. EST (2200 GMT) about its moon base plans. It will feature Fox, García-Galán, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman and Dayna Ise, the acting director of the Utility and Infrastructure Office for the Moon Base Program.

There will also be dramatic flyovers on both days of Max Power, some of them by Isaacman, who's an accomplished pilot as well as a private astronaut. (He funded and commanded SpaceX's Inspiration4 and Polaris Dawn missions, which flew to Earth orbit in September 2021 and September 2024, respectively.)

According to NASA's Max Power schedule, Isaacman will perform flyovers both Saturday and Sunday at 11:58 a.m (in an F-5 jet) and 1:31 p.m. (in a MiG-29).

There will also be a lot to see as you're wandering the grounds at the Max Power sites.

The event "will showcase the newest aircraft, autonomous vehicles, technologies, and more defining the future of air and space," agency officials wrote in a Max Power description. "NASA will display its quiet supersonic X-59 plane, and agency partners will showcase moon rovers, spacecraft and more."

Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. To find out what his latest project is, you can follow Michael on Twitter.

#804. Cast your vote for BBC Women's Footballer of the Year 2026

Meet the BBC Women's Footballer of the Year contenders

Voting is now open for the BBC World Service Women's Footballer of the Year 2026.

Fans worldwide can vote from the five-player shortlist of Temwa Chawinga, Ewa Pajor, Alexia Putellas, Alessia Russo and Khadija 'Bunny' Shaw.

The vote closes on Wednesday, 18 November at 09:00 GMT.

For the first time in the award's history, the winner will be announced as part of the BBC's Sports Personality of the Year on Sunday, 13 December as well as on the BBC World Service and the BBC Sport website and app.

Contenders for the award - now in its 12th year - are nominated by coaches, journalists and former professionals. It covers the period September 2025-August 2026.

Cast your vote, and read more on the five contenders.

Sorry, this vote cannot be loaded. In order to vote you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.

Listen: Who is your BBC Women's Footballer of the Year 2026?

BBC Women's Footballer of the Year contender Temwa Chawinga

Chawinga has established herself as one of the world's most prolific forwards.

Her impact on the National Women's Soccer League is clear. Her extraordinary form helped Kansas City Current clinch the NWSL Shield as the league's top team in the regular season.

Chawinga scored 15 goals in the 2025 season as she became the first player to be named NWSL MVP in back-to-back campaigns. She also won the Golden Boot for the second year in a row.

Those performances earned her a contract extension through until 2029.

Chawinga returned to international football with Malawi for the 2026 Women's Africa Cup of Nations.

Alongside her sister Tabitha, she helped Malawi reach the country's first Wafcon final and - in doing so - qualify for the Women's World Cup for the first time.

Chawinga scored against Nigeria, Egypt, Ghana and Algeria at Wafcon, winning the tournament's Golden Boot with five goals.

BBC Women's Footballer of the Year contender Ewa Pajor

Pajor is widely regarded as a world-class number nine - and it's clear why.

Instrumental as Barcelona won four trophies last season, Pajor scored their first two goals in a 4-0 Champions League final victory over Lyon.

The goals meant she finished as the competition's top scorer, while the result meant she won the Champions League for the first time after losing in five finals - four with Wolfsburg and one with Barcelona.

Pajor also enjoyed an outstanding second season with Barcelona in Liga F, scoring 16 league goals in her 23 appearances and providing five assists. She was a key player as Barca won the domestic treble.

On the international stage, Pajor captains Poland as is the team's leading goalscorer.

BBC Women's Footballer of the Year contender Alexia Putellas

Club: London City Lionesses Position: Midfielder

Putellas showed again this year why she is one of the most influential footballers in the world.

After 14 years with Barcelona, she delivered a spectacular final season with the club - helping them win four major trophies.

Her 14 goal contributions in 11 Champions League appearances helped her childhood club win the competition for the fourth time, and she remained a decisive figure bringing experience and leadership when it mattered most.

Putellas delayed announcing her move to London City Lionesses to avoid creating a distraction, but in July 2026 she completed that transfer, saying the club's "women-only identity and ambition" were important factors.

Internationally, Putellas was instrumental in Spain retaining the Women's Nations League in late 2025, scoring three goals against Sweden in the semi-finals before being named player of the finals as Spain defeated Germany 3â0.

Last month she was awarded a record-equalling third Ballon d'Or.

BBC Women's Footballer of the Year contender Alessia Russo

Russo has proven to once again be a trusted and integral attacking force for Arsenal, while remaining a key player for England.

She scored 13 WSL goals last season to finish second in the league's scoring charts, and also added six assists in her 22 appearances. In total, she registered 24 goals and eight assists across all competitions.

Among the highlights of her season was winning the inaugural Women's Champions Cup with Arsenal, beating Corinthians 3- 2 after extra time.

It was the first competitive trophy Arsenal's women's team had lifted at the Emirates, though they finished runners-up to Manchester City in the WSL.

Russo remains a first-choice striker for England and in April scored her 30th senior international goal to move into the top 10 of Lionesses goalscorers.

She was also nominated for the PFA Player of the Year award.

BBC Women's Footballer of the Year contender Khadija Shaw

After a fine year, Shaw has positioned herself as one of the world's elite forwards.

The defining striker in Manchester City's Women Super League title-winning campaign, she scored 21 goals in 22 league appearances, won a record third consecutive WSL Golden Boot and was named WSL Player of the Season.

Her goals were central to City ending a 10-year wait for the league title.

They went on to complete the Double, with Shaw scoring the opening goal in their FA Cup final victory over Brighton at Wembley to finish the season with 26 goals in all competitions.

She also reached a major personal milestone in December 2025 when she became the first player in the history of City's professional women's team to score 100 goals.

Amid uncertainty over her future, Shaw announced at City's end-of-season celebrations that she had signed a new four-year contract through to 2030.

#803. Gordon Ramsay Shows Off Abs in Shirtless Photo for 60th Birthday

Gordon Ramsay celebrated his new decade of life with an egg-cellent shirtless pic that showed his life is getting butter with age.

Gordon Ramsay is only getting better with thyme.

The Hell’s Kitchen star celebrated the day after his 60th birthday with a steamy shirtless picture that has so much heat you nearly have to stay out of the kitchen.

In the Nov. 9 Instagram picture, Ramsay proved that, unlike his vegetables, he is not chopped as he stood nearly-naked in his workout gear and flexed for the camera, showing off his toned physique.

The chef—who trains for his triathlons with cardio and daily pushups—paired his post with a side of gratitude, writing in the caption, “Thank you everyone for the incredible birthday messages! Day 2 of being 60……LFG!!!!”

The day before, Ramsay commemorated his birthday milestone by celebrating his daughter—and birthday twin—Tilly’s 25th stir around the sun.

“Happy birthday to this incredible young lady,” he wrote on Instagram alongside throwback pictures with his (tater) tot. “Sharing such a special day with you is a Dads dream, there’s not enough words to explain how proud you make me feel.”

Ramsay added, “Have a fantastic 25th birthday and I can’t believe I’m bloody 60 wtf.”

But while he may be known for his strict personality on TV, the MasterChef host—also dad to kids Megan, 28, Jack, 26, Holly, 26, Oscar, 7, and Jesse, 2, with wife Tana Ramsay—has explained that his harsh demeanor is boiled down to a reduction when he’s at home with his family.

“The kids have brought the most emotion out of me,” he told People in 2023. “It’s funny, isn’t it? Because everyone thinks, ‘God, you must be an absolute ass to be at home with.’ [But] Tana’s super fierce, an ex-Montessori school teacher. So I’m the softie.”

In fact, Ramsay’s daughter Holly—who tied the knot with Olympic swimmer Adam Peaty in December—quipped that he would need more than a dish towel on her wedding day.

“The day he walks me down the aisle, we are going to need so many tissues,” she added to People. “My veil will have to be [made of] tissues so he can walk behind me and mop up his tears.”

#801. Hill gets first England call-up as Konsa cover

James Hill has played for England Under-20s and U21s

Bournemouth defender James Hill has been called up to the England squad for the first time.

The 24-year-old centre-back has been added to Thomas Tuchel's squad after Arsenal's Ezri Konsa was ruled out of Thursday's Nations League match against Croatia at Wembley.

Konsa was substituted after sustaining a knee injury in the Champions League win at Slavia Prague on Wednesday, but played all 90 minutes of the win over Hull on Saturday.

He will return to full training this week, before England's game against Spain in Madrid on Sunday.

On Sunday Dan Burn replaced centre-back Marc Guehi, who withdrew with a hip injury.

Hill has played every minute of Bournemouth's Premier League season and has featured in every game of their inaugural Europa League campaign.

He joined Bournemouth from Fleetwood for an undisclosed fee in January 2022.

Having made only 24 appearances in his first three and a half years with the club, Hill became a regular last season as Bournemouth achieved their highest top-flight finish of sixth.

Bournemouth, who are on an eight-match winning run in all competitions, are seventh in the Premier League.

A colossal coronal hole on the sun is unleashing a stream of high-speed solar wind that could spark impressive auroras Nov. 6-8.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The northern lights could put on an impressive display this weekend as a colossal coronal hole on the sun fires a stream of high-speed solar wind toward Earth. Minor (G1) geomagnetic storm conditions between Nov. 6 and Nov. 8, with a chance of moderate (G2) conditions on Nov. 7 and Nov. 8, according to NOAA's Space Weather Prediction Center (SWPC).

If G2 conditions materialize, the northern lights could be visible as far south as New York and Idaho.

The culprit behind the potential uptick in northern lights is a large coronal hole on the sun, a region where the sun's magnetic field opens up. They allow streams of charged particles known as the solar wind to escape more easily into space. Coronal holes appear darker in ultraviolet images because they are cooler and less dense than their surroundings.

And this particularly large — and rather oddly shaped — coronal hole is sending some seriously speedy wind our way.

The U.K. Met Office forecasts solar wind speeds between 342 and 404 miles (550-650 kilometers) per second, considerably faster than the typical speed of around 249 miles (400 km) per second.

The fast solar winds are expected to arrive around Nov. 6-7 and could persist through much of the weekend. It could interact with Earth's magnetic field, potentially triggering geomagnetic storms and fueling spectacular aurora shows. The stronger the storm, the farther south the northern lights can potentially be seen.

Under G1 conditions, auroras may be visible from northern Michigan and Maine, but if activity intensifies to G2 levels, skywatchers farther south, including those in New York and Idaho, could be in for a treat.

But remember! Aurora forecasts are notoriously tricky. Much depends on the strength and orientation of the magnetic field carried by the incoming solar wind, particularly whether it points southward, allowing more energy to transfer to Earth's magnetic field.

To give yourself the best chance of seeing the northern lights, keep an eye on those aurora forecasts, head somewhere dark away from city lights if you can, with a view of the northern horizon. To stay updated on space weather and know the best times and places to catch auroras, consider using a space weather app tailored to your location. One app I recommend is "My Aurora Forecast & Alerts," available on both iOS and Android. Another great tool is the "Space Weather Live" app on iOS and Android, which offers more in-depth insights into current space weather conditions and their potential for aurora activity.

Daisy Dobrijevic joined Space.com in February 2022, having previously worked as a staff writer for All About Space magazine. She completed an editorial internship with BBC Sky at Night Magazine and worked at the National Space Centre, communicating space science to the public.

Daisy holds a PhD in plant physiology and a Master's in Environmental Science. Based in Nottingham, U.K., she covers all things space, with a special focus on solar activity and space weather. She also has a keen interest in astrotourism and is always on the lookout for the next northern lights adventure.

She will join Hurtigruten as an onboard astronomer for a northern lights sailing in January 2027.
