#797. Pete Davidson Says Ex Elsie Hewitt “Crushed” This Part of Halloween

Pete Davidson shared insight into his Halloween reunion with ex Elsie Hewitt, confirming she played an important role in their daughter Scottie’s Sopranos-themed costume.

You don’t got to love this costume choice, but you will respect it.

When it came to celebrating his daughter Scottie’s first Halloween, Pete Davidson knew he had to dress her up as the protagonist of his favorite TV show, Tony Soprano. As for their Sopranos-themed costumes, the SNL alum said it was his ex Elsie Hewitt who best steered that ship.

“We had a great time,” Davidson told Jimmy Fallon during his Nov. 9 appearance on The Tonight Show. “And I’ve got to give Elsie credit, she did the whole wardrobe. She crushed it.”

After all, not only was Scottie outfitted in a bathrobe, gold watch and fake cigar plus slicked back hair to complete her Tony costume, but Davidson and Hewitt rounded out the Soprano clan as Paulie Walnuts and Christopher Moltisanti, respectively.

As for why the pair landed on the James Gandolfini character for the 10-month-old’s Halloween debut?

In addition to being the “biggest Sopranos guy,” Davidson revealed, “Before she was even born me and Elsie were like, ‘We gotta.’ Because her hair’s gonna grow. She’s got the perfect Tony hair, because she has no hair. It’s the only year we could.”

And though the How to Rob a Bank star admitted Scottie “hated” dressing up as the head of the Soprano family, he’s still hoping to instill a love of the mafia show from an early age—without exposing Scottie to the bloodier aspects of the series.

“Sometimes when she's playing, I'll play The Sopranos in the background so she gets used to Tony's voice,” Davidson revealed. “Because my sick head thinks, ‘Well, when she's older, she'll be like, “Oh.’” It'll be familiar.”

But in the meantime, even though Scottie is years away from being able to tune into the drama of the DiMeo crime family, there’s nowhere that Davidson would rather report live from than at his daughter’s side.

As he said of fatherhood, “It’s the best.”

For Hewitt and Davidson, Halloween fell about five months after they parted ways as a couple. Despite the breakup, however, the pair reunited to give Scottie a seamless holiday experience.

In fact, Hewitt gave an up-close look at their night out on Oct. 31, which saw the pair parade Scottie around in a Sopranos-decorated wagon.

The European Space Agency's (ESA) Hera spacecraft has gotten its first close-up look at the Didymos binary asteroid system. If that system sounds familiar, it's because it made headlines in September 2022 when NASA's DART (Double Asteroid Redirection Test) spacecraft smashed into it.

The aim of the DART mission was to test whether an impact could divert an asteroid away from a collision course with Earth. The purpose of Hera is to follow up on DART by making up-close observations of the Didymos system.

"The first thing we said was, 'Wow,'" Hera Principal Investigator Patrick Michel said in a statement about the image, which ESA released on Thursday (Nov. 5). "This is the other side of Didymos from the one that DART’s camera showed us shortly before impact, so this feels like looking at a whole new world."

The Didymos system consists of the eponymous 2,560-foot-wide (780 meters) space rock and its "moonlet" Dimorphos, which is about 530 feet (160 m) in diameter.

The DART mission impacted Dimorphos on Sept. 26, 2022, with the aim of causing a change in the orbital period of the moonlet. And it worked: Before the impact, Dimorphos completed one lap around Didymos in around 11 hours and 55 minutes. The DART collision reduced the length of this period by around 33 minutes.

The change is a result of the fact that Dimporphos is now traveling at around 2.7 millimeters per second more slowly than it did before the collision.

The newly released photo shows Didymos in detail. Just a sliver of Dimorphos is visible, below and slightly to the left of the main asteroid.

The changes caused by DART were small. But in a real Earth-threatening scenario, even such a tiny shift could help divert an asteroid on a collision course — as long as scientists get enough advance warning of its approach.

Hera's observations should help reveal what other changes have occurred on and around Didymos.

Scientists are already seeing that, while Didymos has the same central ridge along its equator as before the impact, many changes have occurred. This includes the creation of multiple boulders, craters, and patterns of grooves or ridges.

"Since we expect a lot of impact-ejected material to have made it across the approximately 1 kilometer [0.62 miles] of space from Dimorphos to Didymos, it may be that some of these characteristics originate from this transport of material, and we have exciting work ahead of us to sort it out," said Michael Kueppers, ESA’s Hera mission scientist. "We look forward to seeing much more of both bodies and systemically mapping all the changes we identify."

#792. Fall Out Boy Announce 2027 World Tour With The Offspring, Good Charlotte & More

The 36-date Twilight of the Punks Tour hits European arenas in May before a 21-show North American stadium run.

Fall Out Boy have announced the Twilight of the Punks Tour on Monday (Nov. 9), a 36-date global run across stadiums and arenas in Europe, the U.K. and North America in 2027. They’ve also released “ACES,” their first new original single in more than three years, via Atlantic Records. Explore Fall Out Boy See latest videos, charts and news

The Live Nation-promoted tour opens May 17 at Prague’s O2 Arena and runs 15 dates through 11 European and U.K. countries, taking in Budapest, Milan, Madrid, Lyon, Brussels, Mönchengladbach, Glasgow, Dublin and Manchester. The leg peaks June 5 at London’s Tottenham Hotspur Stadium and wraps June 13 at Atlas Arena in Łódź, Poland. A Day to Remember and Neck Deep support throughout. North America follows with 21 stadium dates, opening July 13 at Globe Life Field in Arlington, Texas, and closing Aug. 26 at Providence Park in Portland, Ore. The run includes Toronto’s Rogers Stadium, Boston’s Fenway Park, Citi Field in Queens, Dodger Stadium in Los Angeles and a hometown show at Chicago’s Soldier Field, the band’s first headline stadium date in the city where they formed. The Offspring and The Story So Far play all North American dates, with Good Charlotte on every show except Aug. 6 and 7.

“ACES” was produced and mixed by longtime collaborator Neal Avron, with a video directed by Brendan Walter. The release lands as the band marks 25 years together.

The rollout leaned on an elaborate online build. Fall Out Boy began teasing in late October with a post about a fictional “Twilight Town Mall,” then rebuilt their website as an interactive shopping directory. A “Two Quarters Arcade” followed, built with Brooklyn agency LOOP, letting fans remotely operate a real claw machine to win a band-branded plush. The band says it drew close to a million site visits and 6.1 million minutes of watch time, and crashed their servers.

Tickets go on general sale Thursday (Nov. 12) at 10 a.m. local time in North America and noon local in Europe and the U.K., with most markets excluding Lyon, Brussels, Paris and Łódź, which follow Friday (Nov. 13). An artist presale begins Wednesday (Nov. 11), alongside a Reserved by Spotify presale in select North American markets.

Fall Out Boy have four No. 1 albums on the Billboard 200, three of them consecutive: Save Rock and Roll, American Beauty/American Psycho and M A N I A, which earned a Grammy nomination for best rock album. Their most recent album, 2023’s So Much (For) Stardust, debuted at No. 1 on Top Rock Albums, and its lead single “Love From the Other Side” became their first No. 1 on Alternative Airplay. In 2021 they co-headlined the Hella Mega Tour with Green Day and Weezer.

#791. Why your physics project needs an anthropologist

Jaco de Swart is a historian and anthropologist of science at the University of Cambridge, UK.

The TAMBO team assesses suitable observatory sites in the Andes Mountains of Peru.Credit: Jaco de Swart

It is uncommon for a social scientist to have a seat at a meeting about an astronomical observatory, let alone for them to jointly lead one. For one-quarter of attendees to be social-science scholars is almost unprecedented. But that’s exactly what happens at meetings about the Tau Air-shower Mountain-based Observatory (TAMBO), a proposed detector to be built in the Peruvian Andes to look for cosmic particles called tau neutrinos.

Space diplomacy: bridging the operating gaps between myriad missions

Space diplomacy: bridging the operating gaps between myriad missions

Tau neutrinos are elusive fundamental particles that are transmitted through space from black holes and other distant sources. When these particles interact with rocks on Earth, they can produce a shower of other, short-lived particles. The idea behind TAMBO is that if such a shower were emitted from one side of a deep canyon, it could be picked up by an array of 5,000 detectors on the other side (TAMBO collaboration. Nature Astron. 10, 947–951; 2026). The Andes Mountains of Peru contain many promising sites.

For those who live in the area, however, the case for TAMBO is less clear. The Andes are a sensitive ecological environment and home to Indigenous farming communities that consider the mountains sentient beings that are integral to their society. The area is also affected by legal and illegal mining, large-scale infrastructure projects and legacies of colonialism. This all leads to scepticism towards large projects that are developed by people from outside the area.

I am the co-principal investigator of the TAMBO collaboration, alongside Peruvian neutrino physicist Carlos Argüelles at Harvard University in Cambridge, Massachusetts. I lead the social-science and ‘responsible siting’ side of the project. Having received funding to build a proof-of-principle experiment called TAMBITO, we are searching for a potential location for the observatory.

Developing astronomers in Africa: ‘We wanted to create a discipline’

Developing astronomers in Africa: ‘We wanted to create a discipline’

Since 2024, the TAMBO collaboration has built partnerships with 11 Peruvian institutions, which are involved in the design and development of the telescope. Scientific links are an important starting point, but they are not enough. No matter what their discovery potential is, big scientific experiments are not beneficial to everyone. For example, construction of the Thirty Meter Telescope has been stalled since 2015 because of protests triggered by objections to its planned site on Maunakea in Hawaii — a mountain that is sacred in Native Hawaiian culture.

To integrate environmental care into the project and build good relationships with the communities that might host the telescope, TAMBO brought in experts on the Andean region. In 2024, the collaboration held a workshop at Harvard’s Radcliffe Institute for Advanced Study, at which scholars and policymakers discussed what equitable astrophysics in Peru would look like. This led to the formation of a responsible-siting team that includes geographers, sociologists and anthropologists who have worked in the Andes.

IceCube just won a Nobel prize. Protect astroparticle physics projects with the same potential

IceCube just won a Nobel prize. Protect astroparticle physics projects with the same potential

#790. Giant exoplanet emerges from the dark when the James Webb Space Telescope turns out the starlight

"We showed that we can actually recover a planet that people previously couldn’t see."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Sometimes science can seem really counter-intuitive. For example, occasionally in astronomy, you can see more with less light. Case in point: the emergence of a giant planet in observations made by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), when astronomers found a way to block out light from the planet's parent star.

The extrasolar planet, or exoplanet, in question is 51 Eridani b (51 ERI b), a gas giant with the same mass as around 11 Jupiters that orbits a star located around 97 light-years away. 51 ERI b was discovered back in 2015 by ground-based telescopes, but the planet was missing from observations of the system made by the JWST. That wasn't a failing of the JWST itself; no one is doubting the observing capabilities of the most powerful telescope humanity has ever hoisted into orbit around Earth. Instead, it was a result of starlight from the star 51 ERI A obscuring this intimidatingly massive world.

The brightest planets are 100,000 times fainter than their host stars, meaning spotting them is like observing a firefly hovering around a lighthouse. Even using a tool called a coronagraph to block the star isn't enough to reveal the planet, as that doesn't stop all the starlight.

The only solution to this glaring problem is a computer program to wipe out the starlight. "For the past 20 years, astronomers have tackled this problem by observing a different star and using its image as a reference," Jason Wang of Northwestern University explained in a statement. "Then, they subtract that reference image from the original observation to remove the unwanted glare to reveal faint planets that otherwise might be hidden."

There is a problem with this process, however. Even the most stable telescopes "wobble." For instance, the JWST requires cryocoolers to keep its NIRCam instrument super cold, and those coolers have little motors that can cause the mirrors to vibrate. This movement, however slight, causes a scatter in starlight. The result is enough glare remaining to obscure a planet, but Wang and colleagues developed a new approach to this problem.

The new approach taken by the team is dubbed Physics-based Learning for Imaging Planets (FLIP), and it involves creating a digital "twin" of a telescope. Essentially a virtual replica that simulates how starlight travels through the telescope's mirrors and reaches its detectors.

This twin is then fine-tuned to account for millions of tiny imperfections in the original telescope. The digital twin is then tweaked until it aligns with observations from the actual telescope. Astronomers can then remove the simulated glare from the original image.

To assess the validity of the technique, the researchers took a second look at JWST observations of two star systems with known exoplanets, HIP 65426 and 51 Eridani, and one system, TYC 5899, with no known planets.

The researchers found that, in terms of detecting faint exoplanets, FLIP outperformed conventional image-processing techniques two to 15 times. This led to ERI b emerging from data collected by the JWST two years ago.

"We showed that we can actually recover a planet that people previously couldn't see," Wang said. "This is real data in a real scenario. It was science left on the table because we didn’t have the right tools to analyze the data in the most optimal way."

The team hopes that FLIP can now be adopted by other astronomers in a bid to recover hitherto undiscovered exoplanets that have been hidden by the glare of their stars.

This could be a major boon for NASA's proposed Habitable Worlds Observatory, which aims to directly photograph Earth-like planets orbiting distant sun-like stars.

"We know of no planets around other stars that are like those in our own solar system," team leader Rodrigo Ferrer-Chavez of Northwestern University said. "It's not that they don’t exist. It's that we cannot see them.

"Every time we improve our techniques, we discover new types of planets. By finding more planets, we can better understand how planetary systems form and evolve, and ultimately how typical our own solar system truly is."

The team's research was published on Wednesday (Nov. 4) in the journal Nature.

The former America’s Got Talent host recently detailed that a short-lived group chat with Mariah Carey, Brittany Bell, Abby De La Rosa, Alyssa Scott, Bre Tiesi and LaNisha Cole—the six women with whom he shares 12 children—was not the most productive way to communicate.

“Tried it,” Cannon joked during the “On Par or Off The Rails” segment of the On Par with Maury Povich podcast Nov. 9. “Off the rails. Too wild for TV.”

And when host Maury Povich asked if Cannon’s current and former partners get along—Cannon is currently in an open relationship with De La Rosa and Tiesi, while maintaining co-parenting relationships with the other four women—the “Feelin’ Freaky” singer joked, “How do you define get along?”

Despite the joke, Cannon clarified that everyone is “civil,” but “everybody has their own life.”

Nevertheless, the 46-year-old maintained, “Putting them all in a group chat together? Not the best idea.”

Cannon also appeared to tease that his family dynamic will be explored in depth during his upcoming Netflix docuseries, scheduled for release sometime this winter. As he put it when Povich asked him if any of his partners get upset about him spending more time with some than others, he quipped, “It sounds like you’ve seen my docuseries already.”

Meanwhile, Cannon isn’t the only member of his family who has shared perspective on their unusual dynamic. Tiesi—who shares son Legendary Love, 4, with Cannon—recently revealed her one dealbreaker in their romance.

“If he has another baby, I’m outta there,” Tiesi shared during the Oct. 6 episode of the Lip Service podcast. “No more.”

In fact, she admitted the current size of Cannon’s family is already a lot to handle.

“I feel the guilt of not having enough time, having a career,” the 35-year-old explained. “You’ve got The Brady Bunch. We’re not doing 13.”

Trust, it certainly won’t be Tiesi welcoming another child with Cannon. The Selling Sunset alum emphasized she’s doing “everything” to ensure she stays a mom to just one kid.

“Never again, never,” she said of getting pregnant. “It’s a no. I’m a one and done.”

For a deeper look into Cannon’s family tree, keep reading…

Children No. 1 and 2: Moroccan Cannon and Monroe Cannon

Mariah Carey gave birth to her and Nick's twins on April 30, 2011. The two announced their split in 2015 after six years of marriage and finalized their divorce a year later.

Beauty queen Brittany Bell gave birth to her and Nick's first child together, a boy, on Feb. 21, 2017.

Brittany and Nick welcomed their second baby together, a girl, in December 2020.

DJ Abby De La Rosa gave birth to her and Nick's twin boys on June 14, 2021.

Model Alyssa Scott welcomed a baby boy with Nick on June 23, 2021.

However, just five months after the arrival of their son, Nick shared the devastating news that Zen had passed away from brain cancer. "Alyssa was just the strongest woman I have ever seen," he said on the Dec. 7 episode of The Nick Cannon Show. "Never had an argument, never was angry. She was emotional when she needed to be but was always the best mom and continues to be the best mom possible. So I've got to say thank you to my entire family but specifically to Alyssa."

"You never know what someone is going through," he added. "Hug your family. Kiss somebody. Tell them you love them."

Model Bre Tiesi welcomed her first child with Nick on June 28, 2022. The baby boy weighed 8 pounds and 10 ounces at birth.

"I did it. An all natural unmedicated home birth," Bre shared in a July 2022 Instagram post. "This was the most humbling / limit pushing yet awakening and completely empowering experience. I can't thank my team enough for delivering my son safely."

Nick and model LaNisha Cole welcomed a daughter on Sept. 14, 2022.

Brittany gave birth to her third child with Nick on Sept. 23, 2022.

Abby gave birth to a baby girl, her third child with Nick, in November 2022.

Alyssa gave birth to her and Nick's daughter on Dec. 14, 2022.

The model shared an Instagram video showing the Wild 'n Out star helping to deliver their baby. "Our lives are forever changed," she wrote. "Zen is in every breath I take. I know his spirit was with us in the room that morning. I know he is watching down on us. He shows me signs everyday. I will hold onto this memory forever."

She continued, "I will remember the sound of Nicks voice saying 'it's a girl' and the look of everything we've been through flash across his face. I will remember the sound of her crying out with her first breath and feeling her heartbeat against mine. My sweet girl, I got my surprise!! We love you Halo Marie Cannon!"

The Andromeda galaxy is one of the most distant things you can see with the naked eye. The difficult part isn't finding it. It's believing that faint smudge really is another galaxy.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The first time I showed someone the Andromeda galaxy (M31), our conversation did not go quite as planned.

I'd carefully worked my way across the sky, starting from the Great Square of Pegasus and hopping from star to star until I was confident I had the right patch. I pointed the telescope, got M31 in its crosshairs and proudly announced to my wife that I had found the closest giant galaxy to the Milky Way. Would she like to see it?

She then stayed quiet for a little too long as she looked through the eyepiece. Then came an unexpected question. "Is it near that little smudge?" Hmmm. "Err, no. It is that little smudge," I replied.

There was a pause. Of course, I knew exactly what had happened. We'd both seen photographs of M31 — a vast spiral galaxy with a brilliant center, sweeping dust lanes and hundreds of billions of stars. What we were actually looking at was a grayish blur that could easily have been mistaken for a mark on the eyepiece.

That apparent disappointment is now my favorite part of finding Andromeda because the unimpressive smudge is real. The light entering your eyes has been traveling across space for about 2.5 million years. No screen, photograph or telescope is necessary. You are intercepting ancient light in your backyard. Technically, the Triangulum Galaxy (M33), about 2.7 million light-years away, can be seen with the naked eye, so it is therefore the most distant object the naked eye can see. But not mine — I've never seen it. M31 is a much more realistic naked-eye target.

Early November is an excellent time to find M31 from the Northern Hemisphere. It's high and well placed during the evening, and this week the moon is becoming particularly cooperative. New Moon falls around Nov. 9, giving us several evenings with little or no moonlight to wash out faint deep-sky objects.

I usually begin with the star Alpheratz, one of the corner stars of the Great Square of Pegasus. You go two stars left, two stars up, and you arrive at M31. Another route — and a good way to check you're in the right place — starts in Cassiopeia, the distinctive W-shaped constellation high in the northeastern sky on autumn evenings. You can use its second V-shape as an arrow pointing straight at M31.

You can do that star-hop with the naked eye or a pair of binoculars, but M31 is visible to the naked eye only under a very dark sky. However, don't look for a miniature version of the photographs. Expect a faint, elongated patch with a slightly brighter middle.

There's another beginner trap to avoid. Images make Andromeda look compact, but its full apparent extent is enormous — several times the width of the full moon — and our eyes usually pick up only the much brighter central region. Once you know that, the smudge starts making more sense.

I'm going to look for Andromeda this week in the least heroic way possible. No expedition. No mountain-top observing location. No elaborate equipment. I'll wait until it is properly dark, step outside and then use Cassiopeia and the stars of Andromeda to work my way toward M31. I'll then reach for my 10x50 binoculars, which are rarely far from my side after dark, whether I'm at home or traveling. They gather enough light to make the galaxy's bright central region much more obvious without turning the exercise into a technical one.

A really useful skill here — whether looking unaided or through binoculars — is averted vision. Instead of staring directly at the galaxy, look slightly beside it. The more light-sensitive parts of the retina away from the center of our vision can make faint objects easier to detect. It feels slightly ridiculous the first time you do it — deliberately not looking at the thing you're trying to see — but it works.

If light pollution means you need binoculars, that still counts. No one gets a prize for detecting Andromeda unaided. After all, the extraordinary part isn't how you see it. It's what the light has done before reaching you. When those photons began their journey, modern humans did not exist. They crossed intergalactic space for roughly 2.5 million years and ended their trip in your retina. Stargazing is often described as looking back in time. With Andromeda, that phrase stops being a metaphor.

This is the week you've been waiting for if you want to spend time on faint objects rather than fighting moonlight. Without a bright moon overhead, spend some time on Andromeda, but revisit the Double Cluster in Perseus (NGC 869 and NGC 884). Binoculars show it beautifully, and unlike M31, it becomes more obviously crowded with stars as you increase magnification. Two other large, bright open star clusters in this region that look great in 10x50 binoculars are the glittering stars of NGC 752 in Andromeda and M34, a bright, hazy patch in Perseus.

Also keep an eye out for "shooting stars" because the Northern Taurid meteor shower peaks overnight on Nov. 11-12. Rates are low — around five meteors per hour under ideal conditions — so don't expect them to "light up the night sky". But they can produce bright, long-lasting 'fireballs' that can add a bit of pizzazz to a stargazing session.

Now that you've found its jewel, the Andromeda galaxy, it's worth trying to construct the constellation itself. As with M31, start with the Great Square of Pegasus and Alpheratz at its northeastern corner. Although it looks like part of the square, Alpheratz actually belongs to Andromeda. From Alpheratz, follow a curving line of stars away from the square through Mirach and on toward Almach. That gives you the basic shape of Andromeda — not the easiest constellation to imagine as a mythological princess, but a useful chain of stars to learn.

Jamie is an experienced science and travel journalist, stargazer and eclipse chaser who writes about exploring the night sky, solar and lunar eclipses, the Northern Lights, moon-gazing, astro-travel, astronomy and space exploration. He is the editor of WhenIsTheNextEclipse.com, author of A Stargazing Program For Beginners, co-author of The Eclipse Effect, and a senior contributor at Forbes.

Hear Neil Armstrong's son and granddaughter sing a moving tribute to the legendary Apollo 11 astronaut

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Straight from its inspiring live performance at New York City's Carnegie Hall this past April, RadicalMedia's filmed presentation of the immersive living space documentary, "We Chose to Go to the Moon," is finally available for the rest of us to watch.

"We Chose to Go to the Moon" premieres Nov. 10 at 8:00 p.m. ET on PBS, PBS.org, and the PBS app, and we’ve got an exclusive clip to share featuring Mark and Kali Armstrong singing "Flight of Fancy."

With a poignant introduction by Oscar winning director Ron Howard ("Apollo 13"), "We Chose to Go to the Moon" recalls the extraordinary saga of the global space race and Apollo moon landings by actors portraying pivotal persons who made it all happen.

These roles include astronauts Neil Armstrong, Buzz Aldrin, Michael Collins and Ed White, Mission Control trailblazer Poppy Northcutt, "Hidden Figures" mathematician Katherine Johnson and members of the spacefaring families that remained on Earth, including Janet Armstrong and Betty Grissom.

This dynamic multimedia production is directed by Tony Award winner Michael Mayer ("Chess"), combining a unique fusion of theater, concert and documentary storytelling using rare archival footage alongside historic flags and artifacts taken to the Moon and returned home. It also revisits the ill-fated Apollo 13 mission and adds a special tribute to moonwalker Neil Armstrong performed by his son Mark and granddaughter Kali.

"We Chose to Go to the Moon" is created, written and narrated by historian John Monsky and stars Ian Weinberger ("Hamilton"), Skylar Astin ("Pitch Perfect"), Brent Comer ("The Outsiders"), Claybourne Elder ("Company"), Elizabeth Gillies (Netflix's "Dynasty"), Taylor Louderman ("Mean Girls") and Joy Woods ("Galileo"). Finally, Ian Weinberger ("Chess," "Hamilton") pulls it all together by conducting Broadway vocalists and the Orchestra of St. Luke’s in a selection of popular period music showcasing songs such as "Fly Me to the Moon," "Rocket Man," "Space Oddity" and "Sound of Silence."

We hope space fans around the world tune in to experience this sensational stage show that honors America's human spaceflight history!

#781. Warner Chappell’s Guy Moot Becomes First Music Publisher to Receive Music Industry Trusts Award

Mark Ronson presented the honor at a ceremony on Monday (Nov. 9) in London.

Guy Moot, chair and CEO of Warner Chappell Music, has made history by becoming the first music publisher to win the Music Industry Trusts Award (MITS).

Moot received the prestigious honor at a ceremony at London’s Grosvenor House Hotel on Monday (Nov. 9), with musician and longtime friend Mark Ronson presenting the award. The annual accolade recognizes individuals who have made a significant contribution to the U.K. music industry.

The award acknowledges Moot’s illustrious career, which started in record stores and has spanned more than 30 years, and his longstanding advocacy for songwriters at WCM, the global music publishing arm of the Warner Music Group. The event raised funds for two U.K. music charities: The BRIT Trust; and Nordoff and Robbins, the U.K.’s leading music therapy provider.

“To be the first music publisher to receive the MITS is an enormous honor, but this award isn’t really about me,” Moot said at the ceremony. “It belongs to the songwriters I have the privilege of working with every day, to my brilliant colleagues, and to my family, who are with me every step of the way.

“Everything we do begins with a song, and none of it exists without the people who write them. Nordoff and Robbins and The BRIT School remind us what music can do: it heals, it connects and it changes lives. Great music can come from anywhere, and it’s on all of us to keep the door open for the next generation.”

Moot joins a distinguished list of previous MITS honorees, including Annie Lennox, Kylie Minogue, Sir Elton John and Bernie Taupin, Lucian Grainge, Michael Eavis, Pete Tong, Roger Daltrey, Rob Stringer, Emma Banks, Jamal Edwards and Jason Iley. Last year’s award went to Global founder and executive president Ashley Tabor-King.

Established in 1992, the MITS has raised more than £7 million ($9.4 million) for its beneficiary charities over the past three decades. Guests at Monday’s ceremony included Jimmy Page, Tinie Tempah, songwriters Amy Allen and John Ryan, Celeste and Louise Redknapp.

Moot was appointed at Warner Chappell Music as co-chair and CEO alongside Carianne Marshall in 2019 and has overseen deals with songwriters including Dua Lipa, Ed Sheeran, RAYE and Charli xcx, and made deals for major catalogues from David Bowie, George Michael and Madonna. He became the company’s sole chair and CEO earlier this year.

The Unistellar Envision smart binoculars have an augmented reality (AR) overlay that provides smart functionality to 10x50 binoculars, enabling night sky and landmark identification.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I have been waiting to get my hands on a pair of Unistellar Envision smart binoculars since they were announced in 2024. Our editor-in-chief tried an early demo of them last year and said that they felt like something out of Star Trek. He was, of course, referencing the red augmented reality (AR) overlay in the Envisions that can identify night sky targets and landmarks, as well as displaying navigational tools. These are the first pair of smart binoculars that can identify targets in the night sky, such as planets, stars and deep space objects.

The build is solid and while they aren't the most lightweight binoculars, the body is hiding that extra technology that enables the AR overlay in the right hand lens. Each pair ships with a soft carry case, a padded neck strap, a USB-C cable and rubber caps for the eyepieces and lenses.

Pre-order the Unistellar Envision smart binoculars for $1,499 / £1,299

I would highly recommend setting these binoculars up in the daytime, as you definitely need a few minutes to get used to the controls and to perform the diopter adjustment. After powering on, all I had to do was connect the model to the Unistellar app, which recognised the device easily and then watch the onboarding videos. Unistellar also recommends performing a 360-degree calibration before your first use to help ensure the best performance.

You need to have location services set to "always" for the Unistellar app so that it can work out your exact location and give you an accurate reading on the augmented reality (AR) display for locations of night sky targets and landmarks.

I haven't had chance to use the night mode on these binoculars yet, thanks to cloudy skies, but I did use the topographical identification and was impressed with the ease of identifying landmarks around my local area. Besides the night and daytime modes, there is also a navigation mode which displays your cardinal direction alongside degrees of your azimuth and elevation angles.

I had a chance to try out the target lock feature on a geographical landmark with a friend and they found the target easily via the indicator on the AR display. The issue with swapping between two people is that the diopter adjustment only be accurate for one person and I can imagine that constantly changing it during field observation would be annoying. My friend also had to adjust the focus wheel to get the AR overlay sharp enough to read but it was a minor inconvenience.

The controls are intuitive and easy to use once you are used to the placement on the top panel. On the left you have the "next" button for advancing a guided tour to the next target, the "target lock" button and the "mode" button for cycling through the different display modes. On the right is the calibration button for adjusting the augmented reality (AR) display against your real-world view and the power button, which doubles up as a switch to turn the AR display on and off.

I'm looking forward to putting the Unistellar Envisions through their paces as I spend more time with them and get some clear skies to try them out on some stars. I think that these are going to be a great tool for learning my way around the night sky, as well as being invaluable when trying to teach others about constellations and targets. With extra functionality expected in future software updates and a plan to allow third-party app development in 2027, I am excited about the possibilities of the exciting new world of smart binoculars.

Billy Joel will tickle the ivories in public again for the first time in almost two years next month. The “Piano Man” announced on Monday (Nov. 9) that he has booked a gig at Florida Atlantic University in Boca Raton for that is being billed as “Billy Joel: An Evening of Questions & Answers … And a Little Music.” Explore Billy Joel See latest videos, charts and news

Tickets for the Dec. 14 event will be available exclusively to currently enrolled FAU students beginning on Thursday (Nov. 14). Related Dr. Dre Says He's Going 'Off the Grid' for the First Time in His Career: 'I'm Going to Go Away' Tate McRae's 'Housewife' No. 1 on Global Charts for Third Week, Michael Jackson's 'Thriller' on the Prowl Cardi B, Travis Scott, Don Toliver & More to Perform at 'Grand Theft Auto VI' Festival

The return to the stage will mark Joel’s first official public appearance since he announced a diagnosis of the brain disorder normal pressure hydrocephalus, which forced him to cancel his planned 2025 tour and step away from public life.

Joel opened up about the brain disorder during his first-ever line call-in special on SiriusXM’s The Billy Joel channel in September, during which he answered questions about his favorite songs and lyrics and assured fans that he’s doing well despite his health challenges.

“I know people are worried about me because they read that I have a brain disorder, which sounds a lot worse than it actually is,” said Joel, 77, on the special. “I’m OK. My balance isn’t that good. Lost a little bit of my hearing, but that may have to do with my age, too, and the rock ‘n’ roll life and the loud volume probably didn’t help. But I’m fine. I want people to not have to worry about me. I’m OK. And I appreciate your call.”

On the special, Joel also assured a fan who was worried about getting a shunt implanted to relieve pressure and help improve side effects such as balance issues and difficulty walking by telling her that initially he was reluctant to have doctors “drill a hole through” his skull to drain off excess, built-up fluid in the brain. But after researching the procedure, he agreed to it and said his hearing and balance had improved.

While it’s unknown what the “little” bit of music at the FAU appearance will look like, it could mark the first time Joel has performed live since the disorder forced him to cancel his planned 2025 tour. The FAU event will also be the first performance by Joel since the singer hopped on stage in Wellington, Fla. in January to play “We Didn’t Start the Fire” and “Big Shot” with a Billy Joel Cover band.

Last month, Joel told The Hollywood Reporter that he’s been forced to sell off his beloved collection of motorcycles because he’s not allowed to drive anymore. At the time, he also said he was unsure if he’d be able to perform onstage again, saying, “I have to take a series of tests before I know.” He added, “I can’t drive right now. I’m not allowed to drive. And I can’t do performances because what the neurologist told me, every time you do a show, it’s like you’re getting a concussion.”

Spotted a dazzling light in the eastern sky before sunrise? It's Venus, and the planet is only going to get brighter as it heads toward its spectacular peak later this month.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Early morning risers heading to work or school before sunrise are likely to notice a very bright, star-like object appearing low in the east-southeast sky just before sunrise. What is somewhat amazing is that just a couple of weeks ago this object wasn't there at all, but now it literally stands out with such brilliance as to almost command the attention of commuters who might be traveling in an easterly direction to "Look at me!"

The object in question is, of course, the planet Venus, which is currently amid one of its most spectacular forays into the morning sky, literally "vaulting up" into prominence.

On Oct. 24, Venus came to inferior conjunction, passing between the Earth and sun and shifting from the evening into the morning sky. And the view is only going to get better in the days and weeks to come!

In terms of morning visibility, Venus is now in a literal and figurative sense "rising to the occasion." It's now rising before the break of dawn, more than 90 minutes before sunrise. From here on, it will rise three minutes earlier each day, so that by Dec. 17 it will rise 3 hours and 50 minutes before sunrise and blaze in a completely dark sky for more than two hours before the first vestige of morning twilight.

It will reach peak brilliance on Nov. 29, when it will shine at an eye-popping magnitude of -4.9. That's 12 times brighter than its nearest planetary competitor, Jupiter and a full 25 times more dazzling than Sirius, the brightest of all stars. If you live in a rural location with no light pollution to interfere, you might be able to make out that it is casting a visible shadow and if you follow it right on through sunrise, it will be evident to your naked eye in full daylight: a tiny white speck plainly evident against the blue daytime sky.

In a way, we could even regard Venus as this year's version of a "Christmas Star," glowing with stunning radiance ". . . in the east" like the biblical quote mentioned in St. Matthew.

After reaching its high point in terms of morning visibility in mid-December, Venus will start a long, slow slide back toward the sun, rising about 1½ minutes later each morning from New Year's Day through late March. By then, Venus will be coming up as dawn is breaking, roughly 100 minutes before sunrise. Venus will continue to get gradually lower and rise progressively later during the spring and by late June it will be coming up less than an hour before sunrise, ultimately vanishing into the bright dawn twilight by July. Venus will then go on a "summer sabbatical" of sorts and will not reappear again until about this time next year when it will begin a very fine evening apparition.

So, if any of your friends or relatives remark to you that they saw a "strange UFO" on the way to work or school recently, you now can set them straight.

Joe Rao serves as an instructor and guest lecturer at New York's Hayden Planetarium. He writes about astronomy for Natural History magazine, Sky and Telescope, The Old Farmer's Almanac and other publications.

#775. Jordan Fisher Will Step Into Prince’s Shoes (And Strap On A Guitar) For ‘Purple Rain’ On Broadway

The actor says his love for the rock icon's music is "in the marrow of my bones" as he prepares to play The Kid.

Since the July announcement that a Purple Rain musical would come to Broadway (following an out of town production in Prince’s native Minneapolis), plenty of questions have loomed about the production, but none bigger than the obvious: who would take on the role of The Kid, immortalized by Prince himself in the film of the same name? Explore Jordan Fisher Prince See latest videos, charts and news

Billboard can now reveal the answer: Jordan Fisher, the 32-year old alum of the screen and stage who’s played several leading roles on Broadway in recent years, will take on the Purple One’s role when Purple Rain begins previews at the Majestic Theater on March 12, 2027 (an opening date is set for April 12). Related Dr. Dre Says He's Going 'Off the Grid' for the First Time in His Career: 'I'm Going to Go Away' Tate McRae's 'Housewife' No. 1 on Global Charts for Third Week, Michael Jackson's 'Thriller' on the Prowl Cardi B, Travis Scott, Don Toliver & More to Perform at 'Grand Theft Auto VI' Festival

“I’ve been such a fan of his for such a long time, for a myriad of reasons, and with this show everything that I have ever worked on in my career professionally I am exercising at the highest level: every instrument that I can play, I am playing on stage live; every dance move, every acrobatic thing that I can do, I am doing on stage in three-inch heels,” Fisher tells Billboard. “I get to tap into this material that’s so familiar to people, but presented in a way that’s fresh for a new generation who maybe didn’t grow up with Purple Rain or with a real understanding of who Prince is and why he is so loved and respected. He is your favorite artist’s favorite artist. He is your favorite musician’s favorite musician, and that kind of mantle is something that I I take very, very seriously.”

Fisher has taken on increasingly demanding leading roles on Broadway in recent years, including John Laurens/Philip Hamilton in Hamilton, the title role in Dear Evan Hansen, Orpheus in Hadestown, and Antony in Sweeney Todd. But The Kid is his most high-profile yet, a role he’ll originate in a sure to be much-scrutinized new musical. On the day he speaks to Billboard, Fisher — wearing a fresh purple and green manicure, not an homage to Prince but the result of a fun trip to the salon with his nephew — is on a break from rehearsal during the show’s second week of development (rehearsals for the Broadway production officially begin in February). He opened up about why he took on such a monumental role, the time he just missed meeting Prince, and getting encouragement from Lin-Manuel Mirandaas he prepares to lead the band on the Broadway stage.  How did you get introduced to Prince’s music, and why do you think it grabbed you as a young person? I mean, there’s so many avenues that we can go down here. I’m five eight and light skinned-ed; I’m an artist and I’m a multi-instrumentalist and I craft and build and create and produce and write and have a very similar kind of pursuit of new and doing things differently. Of course, by no stretch of the imagination would I ever compare myself or my artistry to Prince Rogers Nelson, but [those similarities have] kind of been impressed upon me for a very long time.  You don’t work in the music industry without hearing people talk about this man and the way that he broke rules left and right and stood up for what he believed in, how he loved his city and and yearned for awareness of the magic that was coming out of [Minneapolis].  The genesis of [my own love of] Prince — my grandfather, who’s no longer here, really loved him. He was the first person to really open my eyes and ears to him and his music. I didn’t really get it when I was younger, and when I when I started digging into it and making [my own] music, people started being like, “Oh my God, you must be a huge Prince fan, huh?” Initially, I was like, “Yeah, yeah, because I’m short and I play a bunch of instruments and we look alike?” But no, it’s all these other things I was missing, and I’ve carried that with me in a massive way.   The very first song of his that I ever heard was “I Wanna Be Your Lover,” and I mean, it’s in the marrow of my bones.  So many people in the entertainment world have a Prince story. In your years working in music in Los Angeles did you ever find yourself in a room with him?  I have a story for you, and it’s just gut-wrenching. I have a friend who had a residency at the W Hotel right across from the Pantages for a long time, and I was there every Sunday pretty much, singing back-up, singing some songs myself, in the midst of auditioning for different things and whatnot. One Sunday I was not there — I was at like, a friend’s wedding or something. [Prince] showed up around 1 A.M. He stood up in the middle of a song — because he’s Prince and he could — and he walked onstage and pointed at the guitar player’s guitar, [and he] realized it was Prince and goes, “Here you go,” and then [Prince] played. It was a moment nobody will forget, and I was not there for it!  But a few years later, I did get a chance to play with Sheila E for a show in LA, and that was the closest that I had been to his artistry and to his excellence, and it oozed off of her, right? That’s the closest I was able to get to him until this [show]. And now I’m like, talking to Bobby Z on a regular basis, and Lisa and Wendy and all of these people that like are in our space here?! Nothing like it.  You were called to audition for this production — did you have any skepticism or did you immediately want to do it?  There is a right way and a wrong way to tell this kind of story, and I think that there’s plenty of right ways to make it happen, but I do think that one of the biggest North Stars is the music and how that happens and how that’s presented. When I got the call, I was like, “Well, I gotta  give this thing a shot.”  When I saw [director Saheem Ali’s] name on the breakdown, I was like, “Oh, they got it right!” Like they got it right because he knows how to keep music at the core and tell a story that is human and tangible and for everyone. Like if you go see Buena Vista Social Club [the Broadway musical, which Ali directed], you don’t need to speak Spanish to understand exactly what’s happening, and that is magic. I have so much love for that man, and  I don’t have enough great things to say about him. He is the perfect director for this.

And then Ebony [Williams], our choreographer, is a commercial dancer and choreographer with commercial background — she approaches choreography from a commercial perspective that’s still driven by storytelling.  And then Jason Michael Webb is our music supervisor, and he and I have worked together a handful of times in the past, and I know his process but more than anything, I know that man is the biggest Prince fan I’ve met in my life.  He’s a walking encyclopedia of Prince. Those pieces right there are the key to presenting this show in the best way possible.  You’ve been lucky enough to do a few big original musicals, including Hamilton, and I know you and Lin-Manuel Miranda are friendly — I’d imagine he’s excited about the idea of a Prince musical?  Yeah he is. He’s got Warriors happening right now too [on Broadway in 2027], he’s in the thick of all of that. But I mean, he’s my homie. I’m hard pressed to think of any human being that could ever give somebody advice on playing Prince on Broadway, but we hung out about a month or so ago. We were talking about it, and he was just like, “Man, I know you’re gonna kill it.” That’s really all that you can say to somebody that’s about to take this on.  Do you feel like Prince’s music is well-suited to Broadway? Prince was probably one of the best musical theater writers that never wrote a musical. His songs have a clear story; there’s a clear “want,” nothing is ever accidental, everything is curated from the lyrics to the notes to the solos to the chord structure to the kind of microphones he used, he had it all down to a science. I wish he could experience the way that his music really tells this beautiful story [in the show]. We’re exploring some of that stuff today [in rehearsal] with “Computer Blue” and “When Doves Cry.” It’s hard to believe that this music works in the musical theater canon the way that it does so successfully. Like it’s not just a jukebox musical; the songs actually carry the show.  How are you approaching the vocals — how much of the “voice” is Jordan vs. Prince? This is a constant conversation. I’m pretty good at impressions, I’m not gonna lie. I’m a nerd and an actor, it’s just part of who I am, it’s like one of my love languages — if I know you and I love you, I’m gonna build an impersonation of you. But the presentation of this — I’m not Prince, I’m The Kid. This is a fictional story, it’s not like a biography of the man.  Therefore, his voice is his voice. My voice needs to encapsulate the essence of who he is but still be a fictional character; otherwise I’m just doing an impression on stage and that isn’t necessarily what we’re going for. The voice he uses in the film doesn’t necessarily work on the stage. So it’s the math of all that, and how do I make it sound like not a musical theater thing but let it have enough presence so that I can reach those people in the back of the mezzanine?  To be continued!

#774. ‘Aroma’ Takes a Sensory Trip Into Loneliness, Fantasy and Forbidden Desire (Exclusive Tallinn Trailer, Chat)

Xue Ma's third feature, a dark fairy tale that blurs the lines between "reality" and the subconscious, including dreams, premieres in Tallinn’s Rebels With a Cause competition.

Her sense of smell dominates Yang’s life. Due to a rare condition, most odors are unbearable for her – except for the smell of lemons and disinfectant. But one day, an unfamiliar scent leads her to a stranger, Fang. It turns out, though, that he is in a coma. Despite his state, Fang is trapped inside – in a life where childhood, fantasy and forbidden desire overlap and blend. His sister, who supported them as a masseuse, returns as a woman in red. And somewhere, the borders between the living, the lost, the dreamed and the imagined are starting to blur for Yang and Fang. Related Stories Movies Claes Bang, Valerie Pachner Drama 'I Is Another' Sells Wide Ahead of AFM Business The Hollywood Reporter Launches Turkish Edition

This is the story – well, part of it – of writer-director Xue Ma’s Aroma (Hõng), her third feature film after White River and Sonata of Wave. If you sense that her new film sounds, looks and feels offbeat, it is just fitting that it will world premiere in the Rebels With a Cause Competition section of the 30th edition of Estonia’s Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival (PÖFF) on Nov. 16.

In Aroma, Jiali Zhao stars as Yang, while Weihao Xu portrays Fang. Ze Ying and Lu Huang also feature in the cast. The cinematographer is Ash Chen, with editing by Maxime Pozzi-Garcia.

The filmmaker “turns smell into an invisible passage between reality and the subconscious,” the PÖFF website teases audiences about the dark fairy tale. “Ash Chen’s hypnotic cinematography gives texture to unstable memories, drawing us from clinical stillness into a dream-world glowing with danger and desire. Sensuous, unsettling and quietly provocative, Aroma keeps its deepest secret just beyond reach. Fang may be trapped inside his fantasy – but what if he is not the only one caught there?”

The filmmaker talked to THR about the themes she explored in the film. But before you read about what she shared below, THR can exclusively premiere the trailer for Aroma. Since the film is created as a stylized feast for the senses, we won’t keep you from watching, hearing and feeling the exclusive trailer. And we wonder if your sense of smell may also get stimulated…

“Cinema lets people experience feelings,” Ma tells THR about her approach to the many sensuous elements that Aroma provides. “I always imagine what cinematic language to use. I think it’s very interesting to experiment and share with others a common [sensory] experience – from the visual and sound to the smell and touch” and to connect that to emotions.

She also tries to surprise audiences. “As an Asian filmmaker, I hope to move beyond the expectations and frameworks through which filmmakers from Asian cultural backgrounds are often viewed internationally,” she tells THR. “I want to create with greater freedom.”

The themes that Aroma explores are also universal, she emphasizes. “Loneliness and something like longing for intimacy is not a matter of language boundaries or [tied to a certain] social and cultural background,” Ma says. “There are people in the world, especially in Asian countries, who cannot express their real emotions and their real emotional needs very clearly. They will hide some secrets. Most people just have this mask. So, actually, I think most of the audience can, in some moments, empathize with the protagonists’ situation.”

And that is particularly true for present-day life. “In this post-pandemic time, this world is very crazy, and I think people can easily feel uncertain and unsettled,” the creative tells THR. “There is a feeling of drifting, so people lose their sense of self and become more acutely aware of their loneliness. The film speaks to the confusion and struggles that anyone might experience beneath their mask.”

The film’s blurring of imagination, reality and dreams is, of course, by design. “All three elements start from human beings,” the Aroma writer-director explains. “So, I don’t think a dream is fake, and reality is real. I think sometimes a dream is more real because there is no need to tell everyone. This is a very secret world. So maybe the dream is more telling about people’s inner side.”

Ma concludes: “I wanted this [cinematic] world to play like a puzzle. Maybe this kind of world can inspire other people to rethink their behavior or what they pay attention to.”

"The Blacklift rocket is the springboard to significantly expand our total addressable market."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Another new private rocket is in the works.

AST SpaceMobile announced today (Nov. 6) that it's building a reusable rocket called Blacklift to launch its broadband satellites to low Earth orbit (LEO), with first flight targeted in 2028.

The news comes just 10 days after Cowboy Space unveiled Big Iron, a rocket designed to launch its constellation of 20,000 AI data centers. Cowboy Space is also targeting 2028 for its first liftoff.

"The Blacklift rocket is the springboard to significantly expand our total addressable market, providing AST SpaceMobile with regular unconstrained access to orbit and providing for most favorable owners’ economics in the industry," Abel Avellan, the company's founder, chairman and CEO, said in a statement today.

"This will accelerate our mission to build a new layer of global connectivity, extending connectivity beyond terrestrial networks and helping to bring AI-enabled services wherever people live, work and travel," Avellan added.

Texas-based AST SpaceMobile is building a LEO constellation composed of its BlueBird satellites, which beam internet service directly to cell phones. The company has launched 13 BlueBirds to date, including eight "Block 2" variants. The antennas on each of these next-gen spacecraft cover a whopping 2,400 square feet (223 square m) — the largest ever deployed in LEO by a commercial satellite.

BlueBirds have flown atop three different rockets to date — SpaceX's Falcon 9, Blue Origin's New Glenn and India's Launch Vehicle Mark-3. But AST SpaceMobile wants to get more vertically integrated, which explains the push to develop Blacklift.

The company won't be starting from scratch. It has signed a deal with another Texas-based outfit, Firefly Aerospace, to provide the engines (and associated engineering services) for the first three Blacklift launches. After that, AST SpaceMobile will build the engines itself, under a licensing agreement with Firefly.

Those engines are Miranda, which will power Blacklift's booster, and Vira, which will power the upper stage.

Neither engine has flight experience. (Firefly's currently operational rocket, Alpha, uses Reavers in its booster and Lightnings in its upper stage.) But Miranda has been tested extensively on the ground, firing for more than 4,200 seconds over the course of 175 hot fires, according to AST SpaceMobile.

"The Miranda engine will allow us to leapfrog the traditional five-to-10-year development cycle as we build Blacklift," AST SpaceMobile President Scott Wisniewski said in the same statement.

The "supply and services" agreement for the first three launches is worth $500 million. The licensing agreement cost AST SpaceMobile about $800 million, with half of that paid in cash and half in stock, according to the statement.

Blacklift will be able to haul 20 tons to LEO. Each launch will therefore be able to loft up to five BlueBird satellites, according to today's announcement. (For perspective: The Falcon 9's LEO lift capacity is about 25 tons.)

BlueBirds will continue going up while AST SpaceMobile gets Blacklift ready to fly: The company already holds contracts with other providers to launch more than 100 of the satellites over the course of 2027 and 2028.

The launch landscape will likely be very different when Blacklift, Big Iron and other new rockets come online. SpaceX has said that it plans to phase out the Falcon 9, as well as its Falcon Heavy heavy lifter, after its Starship megarocket gets up and running.

That milestone could come in the next few years, ushering in something of a launch crunch for satellite operators. SpaceX has indicated that it will prioritize launches of its own satellites with Starship. And there will be a lot of them to loft — 100,000 Starlink V3 satellites and a million Starmind AI data centers, company founder and CEO Elon Musk has suggested.

Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. To find out what his latest project is, you can follow Michael on Twitter.

#771. THE•TEAM Forms New Board Following Sale Finalization

The board's formation follows the finalization of Providence Equity Partners' purchase of the booking agency.

Talent agency THE•TEAM has formed a new board of directors, the company announced Tuesday (Nov. 10), marking the first time it has had a public-facing board.

THE•TEAM, formerly known as Wasserman, was sold by founder and former CEO Casey Wasserman to Providence Equity Partners in July following an outcry after Wasserman’s name surfaced in the Epstein Files. The deal was finalized in October.

Joining the new board are Michael Watts (CEO), Elizabeth Lindsey (global president, brands and properties), Jason Ranne (president, global talent representation), Kevin Shivers (co-president, music), Matthew Vandrau (president, EMEA & APAC), Elena Rochelli (chief financial officer) and Jon Liebman (chairman and CEO, Brillstein Entertainment Partners). Each business leader will continue serving in their roles at the company.

Noell added, “THE•TEAM has an incredibly talented leadership team and we welcome the expertise and perspective that this board will bring to the business. We’re excited about the growth opportunities ahead and will continue to provide capital and strategic partnership to help expand THE•TEAM’s capabilities across sports, music and entertainment.”

THE•TEAM’s music roster includes Chappell Roan, Coldplay, Ed Sheeran, SZA, Kendrick Lamar and Tyler, The Creator, among others.

Accused of sexual assault and grooming, the comedian had sought an injunction that would have prevented ITN and The Guardian from publishing his name — a legal bid he lost.

Comedian and best-selling children’s author David Walliams has been unmasked as the previously anonymous British celebrity accused of sexual misconduct with “a large number of girls and young women.”

The BAFTA-winning star, known for Little Britain, Come Fly With Me and for his 10-year judging stint on Britain’s Got Talent, has been accused of sexual assault and grooming girls as young as 15.

He had sought an injunction to prevent two news organisations, ITN and Guardian News and Media, from publishing his identity, over fears that he would be “highly likely” to kill himself. He maintained that the suicide risk is not attributed to any wrongdoing but because of what his lawyers described as “trial by media.” Related Stories Movies 'Aroma' Takes a Sensory Trip Into Loneliness, Fantasy and Forbidden Desire (Exclusive Tallinn Trailer, Chat) TV BBC Studios Names Sreya Biswas New Head of Its Natural History Unit

He has been unidentified in the press until now, following the judge’s rejection of an injunction last week and Walliams’ refusal to lodge an appeal. U.K. news organizations had been warned against publishing any details that could identify Walliams before the result of the injunction bid came through.

And after failing to meet the appeal deadline on Monday, The Guardian and ITV News released their three-year joint investigation on Tuesday, titled: “David Walliams: Power and Silence.” Walliams is accused of preying on teenage girls and young women for “sexual purposes.” He denies all of the allegations and told the outlets, “I am not a sexual predator… I have not broken the law.” The Hollywood Reporter has reached out to his reps for comment.

One woman described her alleged encounter with Walliams at 15 years old as a “sexual assault,” and multiple women accuse him of “grooming” them when they were teenagers.

The Guardian‘s digital report opens with the testimony of Alex, who was contacted by Walliams when she was 15 and he was 32. “Hi, it’s David Walliams,” she says she remembers him saying over the phone in January 2004. “You know, off the telly!”

She’d met him at a fan event for Little Britain a couple of days prior, she said, where he allegedly told her: “You’re a very attractive lady.” With ambitions of becoming a comedy writer, Alex says she gave him some printouts of scripts she had written and included contact details on the cover letter, not expecting him to reach out. Over the next two years, Alex says she and Walliams spoke on the phone a couple of times and exchanged emails. When she turned 17, they were having sex, she says.

She is one of “multiple women” who allege Walliams “abused his power and position as a celebrity to prey on them for sexual purposes when they were teenagers or young women,” according to the bombshell report.

Most say they were over 18 when they interacted with Walliams. The allegations extend to his conduct in professional environments, with “several sources” describing inappropriate behavior toward women on both Britain‘s Got Talent and his publisher, HarperCollins.

The investigation follows a slew of news stories that have emerged on his behavior in recent years, including his being completely dropped by HarperCollins in 2025. Walliams is one of the country’s best-selling authors, having sold over 50 to 60 million copies of his books worldwide, with Gangsta Granny, Mr. Stink and The Boy in the Dress among his most famous.

But a report in The Daily Telegraph in December 2025 accused Walliams of “harassing” junior female employees at HarperCollins, where former staff said they were told to work in “pairs” when meeting him and advised not to visit his home. He strongly denied the claims at the time.

TMZ recently reported that Walliams had been dropped from an upcoming film, The Road to Nevermore, as allegations of misconduct surfaced. It is unclear if these allegations are connected to the claims made in The Guardian and ITV News.

Then last week came the sudden closure of The World of David Walliams, an attraction at one of the U.K.’s flagship theme parks, Alton Towers. The Merlin Entertainments-owned park said it would permanently close the area, which brought to life the characters from Walliams’ massively popular books, after five years.

“As the 2026 peak season at Alton Towers Resort comes to an end and following our regular review of rides and attractions across the resort, we have taken the decision to permanently close the World of David Walliams,” said a Merlin spokesperson to THR. The spokesperson declined to elaborate but said a range of operational and guest experience decisions were taken into account.

In June last year, Walliams drew widespread condemnation, including from the BBC, for making two Nazi salutes during a recording of the British panel show Would I Lie To You?. He reportedly made the gestures during a segment in which another panellist joked about injuring their wrist while waving. The audience at Pinewood Studios, where the show’s Christmas special was filmed, was reportedly shocked when Walliams joined in to mimic the waves before holding his arm in a Nazi salute.

"These observations were an important piece of evidence that the heavens were not immutable."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Nov. 6, 1572, the German astronomer Wolfgang Schulër observed a supernova with his bare eyes. He spotted the exploding star in the constellation Cassiopeia. It was as bright as Venus and could even be seen during the day.

Astronomers were really confused, because it looked like a star just appeared out of nowhere. Schulër may have been the first to see it, but the Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe is widely credited for the discovery. Brahe studied it in detail and wrote a whole book about this so-called "new star." It then became known as "Tycho's Star."

At the time, supernovas had not yet been discovered. Tycho's Star was finally classified as a supernova in the 1940s. Scientists now think it was a small star called a white dwarf that exploded thousands of years ago. Because Tycho's Star is 13,000 light-years from Earth, it took a while before anyone could see it.

The Tycho supernova, known technically as SN 1572, is known today as a Type Ia supernova, which is a star explosion in a binary star system in which a white dwarf star draws material away from its partner, then explodes. But in 1572, the Tycho supernova appeared as something very different: a bright new star.

While Schulër was first, other astronomers also observed the apparently new star in the sky. Tycho Brahe's numerous observations are the most well known, in no small part becuause he wrote a book all about them in "De Stella Nova" (Latin for "On The New Star." At the time, the prevailing theory among scientists was that the stars were unchanging, yet here was a new star -- a changed sky.

"The 16th century exploding star, which appeared in the constellation Cassiopeia, was seen in daylight for about two weeks, and remained visible to the naked eye for 16 months," the University of California Berkeley wrote in 2004. "Brahe's meticulous record of the brightening and dimming of the supernova now allows astronomers to identify its 'light signature" as that of a Type Ia supernova."

"This was at the end of the Dark Ages in Europe, and these observations were an important piece of evidence that the heavens were not immutable," astronomer Alex Filippenko, who led a 2004 study on the origins of the Tycho supernova, said at the time.

Today, astronomers are closely watching another star that might explode. Called T Corona Borealis, or the Blaze Star, the object is expected to be on the verge of exploding in a nova (a star explosion that is smaller than a supernova and may not destroy the star). is one of 11 known stars observed to have recurring nova explosions within gaps of 100 years or so.

It was SpaceX's 125th launch of the year.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

SpaceX just launched a classified mission for the U.S. military.

A Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from California's Vandenberg Space Force Base this evening (Nov. 6) at 7:48 p.m. EST (4:48 p.m. local California time; 0048 GMT on Nov. 7), rising into the sky as the sun sank toward the Pacific.

The launch kicked off the USSF-432 mission for the U.S. Space Force, which we know little about. Neither SpaceX nor the Space Force told us much about USSF-432 beforehand, and we learned tonight; SpaceX cut its webcast off about 10 minutes into the flight, shortly after the Falcon 9's first stage came back to Earth for a landing.

That touchdown occurred aboard the SpaceX droneship "Of Course I Still Love You," which was stationed downrange in the Pacific Ocean. It wrapped up the eighth flight for this particular booster, which is designated 1095.

The Falcon 9's upper stage, meanwhile, continued carrying its mystery payload skyward. It could be headed to low Earth orbit, outside observers speculate.

"It is possibly a batch of classified LEO satellites for the USSF's Space Based Sensing and Targeting (SBST) portfolio based on SpaceX's Starshield satellite bus, based on locations of rocket stage drop zones being exact fits with previous Starlink Group 15 launches," NextSpaceflight.com wrote in a mission description.

Starlink is SpaceX's LEO broadband megaconstellation, which consists of more than 11,000 active satellites. Starshield is a similar system designed to provide services to the U.S. military and its allies. Starshield satellites are believed to be based heavily on the Starlink spacecraft bus.

USSF-432 was the 119th Falcon 9 launch of 2026, and the 14th national-security flight of the rocket so far this year. The vast majority of Falcon 9 missions in 2026 — more than 70% — have been devoted to building out the Starlink megaconstellation.

SpaceX has also launched six other missions this year. Three were operational flights of the company's Falcon Heavy rocket, while the other three were test missions of its next-gen Starship vehicle. SpaceX plans to retire both the Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy shortly after the fully reusable Starship, the biggest and most powerful rocket ever built, is up and running.

Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. Rom-com queen Lana Condor and husband Anthony De La Torre are set to star in The Receipt, a six-part holiday-themed microseries with brand partnerships from Fetch, the rewards app.

All the Boys I’ve Loved Before star Condor will play Chloe who after a holiday tote bag mix-up has to find Max, a mysterious stranger, with the help of Liam, her best friend played by digital content maker Eric Sedeño. Chloe begins piecing together Max’s identity via clues from his everyday purchases.

“We wanted to make something people would genuinely want to watch, not something that felt like an ad they had to sit through. The Receipt has all the ingredients of a classic holiday rom-com – a missed connection, a little mystery, and a love story you want to root for. Think Cinderella meets Hallmark, but told in short episodes designed for the way people watch today. And because it’s Fetch, we’re giving audiences a way to get rewarded along the way,” Spychalski said in a statement.

The holiday romancer will launch on the Fetch app and social media platforms and will see brand partners including Dove, Betty Crocker and Breyers woven into storylines for episodes each to last two to four minutes.

That will allow viewers of the ultrashort comedy product offers and rewards via the Fetch app. They will earn Fetch Points by watching episode clips in the app and making qualifying purchases of featured products, before then redeeming points for gift cards.

The Receipt promises a new branded entertainment model for how marketers, content creators and the traditional entertainment industry can work together, Spychalski added.

“It’s no longer enough to put your product in a scene and hope people notice. The opportunity is to help create something audiences actually care about. With The Receipt, brands like Dove, Betty Crocker and Breyers are woven authentically into the story itself, and Fetch extends that connection beyond the screen and into the shopping experiences people have every day. That’s a much more interesting relationship that drives real outcomes between a brand and its audience,” he argued.

The Receipt also looks to leverage industry trends towards the emergence of social-first scripted content, digital creators and influencers and major brands investing in entertainment to reach consumers.

Sedeño explained co-starring in The Receipt is part of the creator economy emerging from YouTube and other online platforms drawing eyeballs form traditional linear TV channels and streamers.

“What’s really exciting to me is how much the world is opening up for creators. We’re not just making sponsored posts. We’re getting opportunities to act, tell bigger stories, and work with incredible talent. I love that Fetch didn’t just bring creators in to help promote a show. They actually made us part of the entertainment. That’s a pretty exciting evolution, and I think we’re going to see a lot more of it,” Sedeño said in his own statement.

After the launch episode, fresh ones will debut every 72 hours through Dec. 18. Fetch as a rewards app for consumers and brands allows users to earn points from everyday activities, including shopping, dining out or playing mobile games. Over $100 million in rewards will be redeemed from Fetch this holiday season, the company said.
