"I think the implications are pretty severe, which is why we're taking it so seriously and putting such extreme focus on the mission right now."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman is serious about launching "big rockets" to the moon every single year for the agency's Artemis program. And the new space race with China is fueling that ambition.

"I feel good. I feel like we are certainly on a more achievable path to the lunar surface today than where we were before," Isaacman told Space.com.

We recently sat down with the NASA chief to discuss the state of the Artemis program, and, off the bat, he made it clear that he's confident in the U.S. space program following the success of April's Artemis II mission around the moon. In fact, just prior to our conversation, it was announced that Artemis II commander Reid Wiseman will become the new deputy director of NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory. But the road from Artemis II's success to crewed lunar landings and, later, a permanent moon base will take a lot of launches of NASA's Space Launch System (SLS) megarocket, Isaacman stressed.

"You know, a lot of people, especially in the space community, start getting [into] if the landers are there or not. I don't really care about that right now. What I care about is that we are launching big rockets no less than once a year," he said.

"I think that's imperative for NASA to be doing these deep-space human spaceflight missions right now," Isaacman added. "So, we had a great mission in April of '26. We will launch again in '27."

That coming launch will be for Artemis III, a crewed mission to low Earth orbit that will test docking procedures between NASA's Orion capsule and one or both of the Artemis program's private lunar landers — SpaceX's Starship and Blue Origin's Blue Moon.

"We need to continue to exercise those muscles," he said, referring to SLS liftoffs. "And, honestly, once a year isn't great, either. I mean, I don't think we're going to get back to the early [space] shuttle days, you know, four missions a year. I don't think we're going to get back to where we were with Apollo, but once a year is the minimum … I would testify that to Congress in this role years down the road.

"If NASA is going to be doing deep-space missions, complicated missions, [we should] launch at least once a year and get as much out of it as you can for taking the risk and spending the taxpayer dollars and building towards something greater," Isaacman added. "That's what we're doing with Artemis III, and that's what's going to better prepare us for Artemis IV."

So, how is NASA coping with the challenges that face them as they approach Artemis III ahead of a crewed lunar landing on Artemis IV, which is targeted for 2028? While NASA can learn some lessons from past moon missions with Apollo, today it's primarily relying on the extensive experience and talent within the agency, according to Isaacman.

"Artemis II is very different from Apollo 8, and Artemis III will be very different from Apollo 9," he said. "Our approach is not exactly the same as it was … But what is the same right now? The spirit, the energy, the potential within NASA. The talent of the workforce and industry is no different than the 1960s."

There's another similarity to the Apollo era: NASA has a rival in its race to the moon. While the adversary in the 1960s was the Soviet Union, today the U.S. is competing against China.

"It is a real space race," Isaacman said. But, he added, "this one is very different than the first one."

"Everything is closer than it was, not just in space. I mean, we had the edge in computing [and] every one of the technology domains during the Cold War. Our capabilities were better by a mile," he said. "[But with] China, it's not [like that]. They're very close."

"We're saying we're going to land on the moon at the end of 2028. China is saying by the end of 2029," Isaacman added. "And it's like, Well, are they going to pull it off? Yes, they will. They've showcased their landers, their rovers, their suits, two-launch architecture with built-in reusability."

So NASA is taking the Chinese threat very seriously, according to Isaacman.

"The consequence of getting this wrong, I'm telling you — it's going to be felt around the world," he said. "It will call everything into question."

"Should I be using American superintelligence or AI? Should I be doing Chinese? Should I be buying their computers? Should I be [buying] ours? Buying their cars, their airplanes, their ships? Whose security guarantees to trust?" Isaacman added. "I think the implications are pretty severe, which is why we're taking it so seriously and putting such extreme focus on the mission right now. But we have that playbook of success, and I think we will prevail."

Chelsea Gohd served as a Senior Writer for Space.com from 2018 to 2022 before returning in 2026, covering everything from climate change to planetary science and human spaceflight in both articles and on-camera in videos. With a M.S. in Biology, Chelsea has written and worked for institutions including NASA JPL, the American Museum of Natural History, Scientific American, Discover Magazine Blog, Astronomy Magazine, and Live Science. #759. Jordan Fisher Takes on Prince’s Role in Broadway Adaptation of ‘Purple Rain’

Fisher will star in the new musical after leading roles in 'Moulin Rouge!' 'Hadestown' and more.

Jordan Fisher will star as “The Kid” in the Broadway stage adaptation of Purple Rain.

A Broadway veteran, known for his starring roles in Moulin Rouge!, Hadestown and Dear Evan Hansen, Fisher takes on the role played by Prince in the 1984 film. The musical is set to start previews March 12, 2027 at the Majestic Theatre, ahead of an April 12 opening.

An alternate performer to be announced will play the role of “The Kid” on Tuesday evenings and Wednesday matinees. Additional casting will be announced at a later date.

The musical, based on the film, features music by Prince, including “When Doves Cry,” “I Would Die 4 U,” “Take Me with You” and “Purple Rain.” The musical follows a young performer known as “The Kid,” who tries to lead his band to fame, while dealing with his own turbulent past, a rival singer and a developing romantic interest.

In addition to his Broadway credits, which also include Laurens/Philip in Hamilton and Anthony in the most recent revival of Sweeney Todd, Fisher has starred on screen in Netflix’s Hello, Goodbye, and Everything in Between, To All the Boys: P.S. I Still Love You, Work It, Rent: Live!, Grease: Live!, and Disney/Pixar’s Turning Red.

“We know that Jordan Fisher is an extraordinary talent, but what’s been thrilling about watching him inhabit ‘The Kid’ is discovering the fire beneath the surface: the swagger, vulnerability and restless creative spirit we recognize in Prince,” said director Saheem Ali. “Jordan brings all of that to the role, along with an infectious generosity that makes everyone around him better. He’s finding something raw, surprising, and deeply human in this iconic character, and I can’t wait for Broadway audiences to experience it.”

The musical comes to Broadway after a world premiere at the State Theater in Minneapolis in fall 2025. The show has since revamped its creative team, with Ali (Buena Vista Social Club) now directing the musical and a new book by Peter Duchan (Dogfight). Choreographer Ebony Williams remains (Sneakerella; additional choreography for the Renaissance World Tour). Kris Kollins, a D.C-based singer songwriter, played the role of the Kid in Minnesota.

Bobby Z and Morris Hayes, both of whom worked with Prince, are music advisers on the production. Orin Wolf, producer of Buena Vista Social Club, is lead producing.

#758. It’s Looking Like Oasis Will Skip Their Own Rock Hall of Fame Induction: ‘It’s Too Far To Be Going For the Night’

Noel's got a gig in London and Liam said it's too close to Christmas to travel.

It should come as no surprise to longtime Oasis fans that Noel and Liam Gallagher‘s masterplan for this weekend’s Rock & Roll Hall of Fame induction ceremony is to definitely, not even maybe make an appearance. The Brit Pop icons have made no secret about their listless attitude about being inducted this year alongside Billy Idol, Joy Division/New Order, Phil Collins, Wu-Tang Clan, Luther Vandross and Sade. Related Dr. Dre Says He's Going 'Off the Grid' for the First Time in His Career: 'I'm Going to Go Away' Tate McRae's 'Housewife' No. 1 on Global Charts for Third Week, Michael Jackson's 'Thriller' on the Prowl Cardi B, Travis Scott, Don Toliver & More to Perform at 'Grand Theft Auto VI' Festival Explore Liam Gallagher Noel Gallagher Oasis See latest videos, charts and news

And, after Rolling Stone reported on Monday (Nov. 9) that the formerly battling, now agreeable brothers would not be flying to Los Angeles for Saturday’s (Nov. 14) event at the Peacock Theatre, Liam Gallagher appeared to confirm that his ticket is not booked. Responding to the report on X on Tuesday morning (Nov. 10), Liam wrote, “It’s too far to be going for the night I got s–t to do it’s Christmas.”

While the “Supersonic” band doesn’t have any gigs until next May for their Live ’27 tour, last week Noel booked his first solo appearance since Oasis’ triumphant 2025 reunion tour with an appearance at Goldie’s EFG Jazz Festival in London on Saturday. At press time a spokesperson for Oasis had not returned Billboard‘s request for confirmation that Oasis would not be present at Saturday’s event.

The brush-off is in keeping with the Gallagher brothers’ indifference to the honor, dating back to their first inclusion on the short list of nominees in 2024, when Liam tweeted, “F–ck the Rock n Roll hall of fame its full of BUMBACLARTS,” later responding to a fan’s suggestion that the band really deserves the honor, Gallagher said, “there’s something fishy about those awards.”

Liam’s stance has remained somewhat steadfast ever since, including in his reaction to Oasis’ second nomination last year, when he reacted on X with the sublime brush-off, “RNR hall of fame is for WANKERS.” His mood was a bit more measured in April of this year, when he said he wanted to thank “all the people who voted for us it’s a real honour ever since I was a little kid and singing in the shower I’d dream about 1 day being in the RnR hall of fame it’s true what they say anything is possible if you have a dream,” a comment that felt like his patented mix of cheek and cheekier. (For context, when a fan resurfaced that comment on Tuesday morning, Liam commented, “I stand by that.”)

In April, a fan asked, “what happened to not wanting to be in it,” to which Liam responded with a story about the siblings’ proper English upbringing. “Well I was speaking to my mummy last night when the news broke and she thinks I may have been a little hasty with my perception of the organization she’s told me to stop being a dick and go to the awards and behave and you never know you might enjoy it,” he wrote, after earlier joking, “reverse psychology vibes in the area Oasis RnR hall of farmers I mean famers.”

At the time, Gallagher confirmed he’d be on hand to accept the honor, writing, “ Too f–king rite I am,” adding that he expected both he and Noel will be there — ”we’re goth going we’re sooooooo proud and humble.”

While it appears the Gallaghers will not make the trip, they will be inducted regardless alongside their bandmates, guitarists Paul “Bonehead” Arthurs and Gem Archer, bassist Paul “Guigsy” McGuigan and Andy Bell and drummer Alan White and Tony McCarroll; at press time it was unclear if the other members of the group would be on hand for the event that will air on ABC and Disney+ in December.

If they do skip the ceremony, Oasis will certainly not be the first band to duck out of collect the honor in person, joining a long list that includes Aretha Franklin (1997), Paul McCartney — who sat out the Beatles’ 1988 induction in the midst of financial disputes with his former bandmates — as well as Tina Turner (1991), the Grateful Dead’s Jerry Garcia (1994), the Sex Pistols (2006), Van Halen (2007), Guns N’ Roses singer Axl Rose (2012) and Dire Straits leader Mark Knopfler (2018), among others.

The movies might be struggling to recapture the magic, but Star Wars video games are strong with the Force.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

After a tumultuous start to EA's rebooted Star Wars Battlefront series, in 2021 Lucasfilm and Disney decided to open up the development of new Star Wars games by bringing in different publishers and studios under the Lucasfilm Games banner. Now, over five years on, we can confidently say we're entering a new golden era of amazing Star Wars games.

With LucasArts' successor calling the shots and coordinating a multitude of projects set in a galaxy far, far away, even EA's latest efforts like Squadrons and the Jedi series have taken bigger and bolder swings. Now, in 2026, the full potential of the Star Wars universe has become clearer with specific releases squarely aimed at niche audiences.

It's become clear that future Star Wars games needn't be expensive endeavors full of familiar faces or concepts. Star Wars Zero Company and Galactic Racer's restrained scope and confidence have been infectious, and, as it turns out, they're already recognized by all the parties involved as double-A success stories.

A Burnout-inspired Star Wars racer (created by a bunch of ex-Burnout devs) is a fantastic pitch if you know your video games, but looking at EA's recent and current direction, it's easy to see why it didn't happen under their reign. The original Burnout studio, Criterion, would have been an excellent candidate, but instead they were sent to work in the Battlefield mines. Still, someone was interested in the idea, and the end result is glorious.

Fast and furious, Star Wars: Galactic Racer ignores recent racing game trends and bets big on arcade-y vibes, uncomplicated controls, and a high skill ceiling that challenges you with extremely high speeds, tight turns, and unexpected interruptions as other drivers try to ruin your day.

The not-so-secret sauce, however, was its runs-based structure, which injects the flexibility and replay value of roguelite games into the more traditional arcade racing structure that older gamers are familiar with.

Fully confident in its central gameplay idea and devoid of modern live-service baggage, Fuse Games' debut title makes the most of the Star Wars setting within the restrictions of simply making a fun and engaging Star Wars racer.

It's almost the same approach we felt in Zero Company, a turn-based tactical strategy-RPG that comes from the minds of another team of ex-triple-A developers. "Star Wars but XCOM" should've happened earlier, but we're glad it did this year, and, unsurprisingly, it's a banger.

The correct read of their success should be obvious (and so far, it appears the powers that be are seeing it): Let seasoned and fresh developers cook games they're excited about.

Big, medium, or small, players will react positively to experiences that really feel genuine and aren't brought down by tacked-on systems or monetization. Ubisoft's Massive Entertainment also got it right with Star Wars Outlaws, but that ambitious open-world title — hardly a fresh pitch nowadays — also faced high sales expectations due to an inevitably gigantic production budget.

Allowing Star Wars to get weirder and more specific could also help the movie and TV side of things. We know Star Wars has finally locked in clearer big-screen plans for the coming years, and with Disney Plus TV series being seemingly scaled down and targeting more distinct stories better suited for a non-theatrical medium, the crowds' responses to Lucasfilm Games' wins shouldn't be overlooked.

You can't manufacture a viral character like Biddy Blas, arguably Star Wars' most popular new character since Grogu's debut in 2019. It just happens. And it happens naturally if Star Wars is allowed to explore the weird corners of a galaxy.

Devoid of ties to the larger canon and set away from the Imperial era, Galactic Racer makes the post-war period richer by going smaller. It's a reminder of much of the promise introduced by The Mandalorian's first season, before it became distractingly "relevant" to the larger saga.

Even the Clone Wars-set Zero Company keeps things relatively low-profile. Yes, major characters like Anakin Skywalker make cameos, but they don't rob the A-Team and Suicide Squad-inspired tale of camaraderie and subterfuge of its valuable independence. Sure, hits like Andor and Rogue One were obvious inspirations for its tone, but the story stands alone, allowing even Star Wars newcomers to jump in and enjoy it with minimal context.

At a time when giant decades-old franchises often struggle to recruit new fans, the last two Star Wars games reinforce the property's new direction in a medium that can reach more potential Padawans than any other.

The good trick? Just allowing Star Wars to be fresh and smaller — and with no homework required — from time to time. In turn, the larger stories on the horizon will be stronger with the Force.

Command an elite squad in a gritty, authentic Star Wars story set in the twilight of the Clone Wars. Step into the boots of Hawks, a former Republic officer leading Zero Company on a covert operation against an emerging threat that could consume the galaxy.

Available on PS5, Xbox Series X|S, and PC.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer is a ​high-stakes reinvention of racing born in the lawless Outer Rim of the ​​Star Wars galaxy.​​​​

Available on PS5, Xbox Series X|S, and PC.

#755. Skydance Earnings: Wall Street Is Skeptical So Far

Analysts react to the first post-Warner Bros. acquisition quarterly results of David Ellison’s Hollywood giant, with one wondering how this merger can succeed when "so many other major media deals have failed."

Skydance’s first quarterly earnings report after the mega-acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery (WBD) is in. And Wall Street’s take on the results and especially the outlook for David Ellison’s Hollywood giant is … still under review.

The results, posted after the market close on Monday, came a year after Paramount’s first financials under the leadership of Ellison. On the earnings call, the Skydance chairman and CEO expressed bullishness on the creative potential of AI. And he addressed the surprise leadership change at DC Studios, with Marvel alum Jeremy Latcham replacing James Gunn and Peter Safran.

Skydance shares were down more than 2 percent to $8.50 in pre-market trading. So, what did Wall Street analysts take away from the entertainment conglomerate’s first financial and strategic update since the WBD deal close? The Hollywood Reporter is compiling key commentary and thoughts below.

Analyst: Laurent Yoon, BernsteinStock rating and price target: underperform, $6Takeaways: “Trailer Looks Good… Waiting for the Movie” was the title of Yoon’s report following the latest results. “The third quarter was more of a prologue than Chapter 1 of Skydance’s journey following the WBD acquisition,” he wrote. “Pro forma financials with WBD won’t be available until sometime before the fourth-quarter print, leaving us on the edge of how this story could unfold. There are more questions than answers, but we come out net positive.”One of the key questions, or developing stories, if you will, is the studio. “Legacy WBD seems likely to be a drag near-term, particularly in the fourth quarter,” the analyst concluded. “Studio performance has underperformed, with management flagging an up to a around $200 million fourth-quarter profit shortfall from WBD theatrical performance. WBD’s larger linear exposure also remains a likely drag, though it represents meaningful opportunity for operating expense synergies.”So, what will investors need to get more bullish? “The raw ingredients are there to build something better than the individual parts. And we wait for Chapter 1.”

Analyst: Michael Morris, Guggenheim SecuritiesStock rating and price target: neutral, no price targetTakeaways: “Skydance’s first report since closing the WBD acquisition showed continued progress at legacy Paramount and limited incremental detail on the combined company,” Morris wrote in his report entitled “Awaiting Takeoff.” He currently doesn’t have a price target on the stock, citing “the lack of historical pro forma disclosure and no third-quarter operating results for legacy Warner Bros. Discovery.” His rating “balances potential upside from synergies and streaming scale against execution risk and the combined company’s higher leverage.”The analyst also outlined what he is looking for now. “We believe the market has heard the strategy and needs evidence of progress in three areas: 1) a content slate that bolsters confidence in consumer demand for core franchises, 2) the net financial impact of combining HBO Max and Paramount+, beginning with the early 2027 bundle, and 3) management of the declining but cash-generative linear business.”Morris highlighted that Warner Bros. is a work in progress, highlighting that management called the studio on track “with the exception of the near-term film slate.” Noting an up to $200 million fourth-quarter profit impact from films already released this quarter and those still to come, the analyst described the DC Studios leadership change as “the first structural response.” And he added: “The 2027 Warner Bros. slate (Godzilla x Kong: Supernova, Man of Tomorrow, A Minecraft Movie Squared, the Ocean’s Eleven prequel, The Lord of the Rings: The Hunt for Gollum) is where Paramount’s greenlight and marketing discipline should show up.”

Analyst: Doug Creutz, TD CowenStock rating and price target: hold, $8Takeaways: Because the WBD deal closed after the end of the third quarter, the latest results reflect “Paramount Skydance standalone results,” the analyst emphasized, summarizing: “Paramount’s standalone third-quarter adjusted EBITDA of $1.0 billion beat our $947 million estimate on stronger DTC and Studios profit, though revenue of $7.03 billion was below our estimate of $7.13 billion.”The TD Cowen expert also noted that management reiterated its target of at least $6 billion in deal synergies within three years and “gave the first breakdown by category,” namely at least $2.2 billion from corporate overhead, real estate, and facilities, $1.4 billion from technology, $1.4 billion from procurement and vendor management, and $1.0 billion from marketing. About 30 percent of those synergies should be in place by the end of 2027.All that said, Creutz continues to have doubts, sharing this investment thesis: “The risks (leverage, integration) of the combination with WBD are high; we remain skeptical that Skydance management will be able to create value from this deal when so many other major media deals have failed.”

Analyst: Robert Fishman, MoffettNathansonStock rating and price target: neutral, $7Takeaways: “Ghosts of the Past, Present and Future” was the title of Fishman’s report, a timely Charles Dickens reference just before Skydance releases Ebenezer, starring Johnny Depp. “After last night’s earnings report, we get a first glimpse of how Skydance views its trajectory in relation to some … questions [we have previously outlined] but still lots of questions remain.”Among them is whether the merged company can balance cost cuts and growth investments. Looking at the areas that Skydance said it would find efficiencies in, the MoffettNathanson analyst offered: “In theory, savings in these areas should get the company to its synergy targets without dipping into its $30 billion-plus of content spending, allowing it to pay down debt without sacrificing growth. However, as we’ve seen with other media M&A, it is a lot harder to see these cost savings translate into real upside to EBITDA and cash flows, likely forcing the company to limit its content spend growth in the future.”And he highlighted a need for investor and analyst patience for a closer look under the hood until Skydance discloses pro forma financials for its business plus WBD early in 2027. For now, he left most of his estimates unchanged.

#754. Webby Awards Launches IMDB-Like Credits Platform to Provide Verified Recognition for Creators Amid AI Growth (Exclusive)

The long-running initiative celebrating the best of the internet will allow winners, nominees and other honored individuals to claim their work, with Shonda Rhimes and Adam Scott among the founding members.

After celebrating its 30th anniversary earlier this year, the Webby Awards is making it easier for winners, nominees and other honored individuals to make sure they’re properly credited for their work.

The IMDB-like Global Webby Credits Registry allows creators, developers, producers, writers and actors to claim verified profiles documenting their contributions. Though the Webbys have long included these names at the bottom of project pages, the profiles bring together a career’s worth of recognized work regardless of whether the people behind these projects move between different companies. Related Stories Movies Ridley Scott Will Miss Academy's Governors Awards, Accept Honorary Oscar Remotely (Exclusive) Movies 'You Can See Everything' Sweeps Critics Choice Documentary Awards

“The people behind great creative work on the internet have never been harder to find, and they’ve never mattered more,” Webby Group executive director Jesse Feister said in a statement. “The Global Webby Credits Registry puts 30 years of Webby recognition in the hands of the more than 150,000 individuals who earned it, and the thousands who will earn it in the years ahead, giving them verified credentials to build reputation in the AI era.”

As AI becomes a bigger tool in both the discovery of information and the generation of creative work, the Webbys argue these verified credits provide a better way to ensure people are recognized for what they’ve made.

“AI is changing how we discover information, including information about people and their work. Search results are increasingly summarized by AI, and as the technology evolves, we expect more of the ways people discover and evaluate creative professionals to be mediated by AI tools,” Feister tells The Hollywood Reporter. “That makes credible, independent records of people’s work more important than ever. A credit on an award-winning project is a meaningful professional credential, but only if that credit is documented somewhere it can be found and trusted. And as AI makes it easier than ever to produce creative work, having a credible record of what you’ve actually contributed to becomes more important, too.”

A number of Webby-recognized individuals, like Shonda Rhimes and Adam Scott, have already published their own verified profiles as founding members. The launch of the Webbys’ credits platform is also being supported by companies that have won Webbys in the past, including PBS, iHeartMedia and R/GA.

“Behind every great PBS digital experience is a team of talented people bringing our mission to life,” PBS’ vice president, multiplatform marketing and content, Amy Wigler, said in a statement. “The Webby Credits Registry gives those individuals recognition that stays with them throughout their careers. We’re excited to help celebrate their contributions and make their work more visible.”

To claim a profile, eligible individuals can search the Webby Credits database for projects they contributed to, claim the credits associated with their work, verify their identity through LinkedIn and publish their profile. As new work is recognized, the people behind those projects can claim their credits as well.

NASA is asking the public to send their names to Titan for an ambitious mission that will see a flying craft explore the Saturn moon in 2034, if all goes according to plan.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

We still may be some time away from sending humans to distant reaches of the solar system, but you can send your name to Saturn's moon Titan, which has the ingredients of life on its surface thanks to NASA's Dragonfly mission.

Dragonfly is an SUV-sized nuclear-powered rotorcraft that NASA aims to launch towards Titan in 2028. The agency opened a special events page in late October to allow members of the public to put their name on the spacecraft. The names will be put upon a chip on Dragonfly during the spacecraft's assembly, and all names must be submitted before Jan. 15, 2027.

The agency says that the mission has no "ordinary itinerary," as Dragonfly aims to between areas miles (or kilometers) apart after arriving on the surface in 2034. "Nearly a billion miles away, an extraordinary destination awaits. Titan has an atmosphere, rivers and lakes, seasons, sweeping dunes and a landscape rich in organic material," NASA officials wrote in the event page. "Upon arrival in 2034, Dragonfly will fly from place to place on this intriguing world to uncover clues about this remarkable moon, and the chemistry that could help us understand the ingredients for life."

Dragonfly will be one of just a few flying crafts on another world, with the first being NASA's plucky Ingenuity mini-helicopter that arrived on Mars along with the still-running Perseverance rover in 2021. Ingenuity was only designed to make five flights, but made it to 72 until its blades were damaged during a landing on Jan. 18, 2024.

NASA is now planning a SkyFall mission on Mars that would use three helicopters, and which may launch as soon as late 2028 for the Red Planet.

Dragonfly, however, is not the first mission to Titan: that would be Huygens, which operated for just a few hours on Jan. 14, 2005 after deploying from the Cassini spacecraft. Huygens was the first lander on an outer solar system world, and measured Titan's atmosphere and took data from the surface.

For its part, Cassini flew by Titan more than 100 times before the mission concluded in September 2017, providing valuable long-term data about the moon from above. Dragonfly aims to show the moon from up close for about 3.3 Earth years. Its destinations will include dunes and a young impact crater called Selk, according to NASA.

"Dragonfly is expected to make one flight every one to two Titan days, which is called a Tsol and lasts about 16 Earth days," NASA officials added of the mission. Dragonfly will stop at a variety of geologic sites, where it will collect samples of surface material for analysis inside the rotorcraft by a suite of scientific instruments."

Dragonfly's goals include learning more about prebiotic chemistry, or the conditions prior to life arising in a location; figuring out if Titan had habitable conditions in the past; and looking for "chemical indicators" of life based on water or hydrocarbons.

Elizabeth Howell (she/her), Ph.D., was a staff writer in the spaceflight channel between 2022 and 2024 specializing in Canadian space news. She was contributing writer for Space.com for 10 years from 2012 to 2024. Elizabeth's reporting includes multiple exclusives with the White House, leading world coverage about a lost-and-found space tomato on the International Space Station, witnessing five human spaceflight launches on two continents, flying parabolic, working inside a spacesuit, and participating in a simulated Mars mission. Her latest book, "Why Am I Taller?" (ECW Press, 2022) is co-written with astronaut Dave Williams.

#750. ‘Heated Rivalry’ Gets Hands on With 4DX Screenings

The hockey romance series is currently screening in theaters to celebrate a year since the show's initial release.

Ever want to immerse yourself in the world of Heated Rivalry? You’re in luck — the hit hockey romance series is officially headed to 4DX.

Regal Cinemas is partnering with CJ 4DPLEX to bring the final two episodes of Heated Rivalry‘s first season to fans in their immersive 4DX beginning Nov. 16. The 4DX experience features motion-enabled seating and synchronized atmospheric effects, so those wondering what Shane Hollander felt like getting checked by Cliff Marleau in the show’s penultimate episode are in for a treat.

The special event will screen at all 59 Regal 4DX auditoriums nationwide, along with other participating locations in other U.S. theaters. Internationally, 4DX screenings will be available at Cineworld in the United Kingdom and Cineplex in Canada. Related Stories Movies Connor Storrie in Talks to Join Ryan Gosling in Marvel's 'Ghost Rider' TV Gay Immigrant Comedy 'One Baby, Please!' to Hit OUTtv Next Month as Latest Queer Series From Canada

“Fans made it loud and clear that they wanted more Heated Rivalry on the big screen, so we’re turning up the heat,” Regal senior vp U.S. content Brooks LeBoeuf said in a release.

“Episodes five and six bring years of tension between Shane and Ilya to a boiling point, and 4DX takes it all to another level. Together with CJ 4DPLEX, we’re giving fans a chance to feel every hit on the ice, every stolen embrace, and every pulse-pounding moment in between,” LeBoeuf continued. “You may know these episodes by heart, but you’ve never experienced them like this.”

Beginning on Nov. 6 and going through Nov. 30, fans of the show have been able to revisit the series across three paired episode screenings: episodes one and two (“Rookies” and “Olympians”), episodes three and four (“Hunter” and “Rose”) and episodes five and six (“I’ll Believe in Anything” and “The Cottage”). Tickets for the regular release run at $9.99 per screening; however, pricing for the 4DX experience is unclear.

Based on Rachel Reid‘s novel of the same name, Heated Rivalry focuses on the complicated situationship between Shane Hollander, played by Hudson Williams, and Ilya Rozanov, played by Connor Storrie. The pair are generational talents in the world of professional hockey and sworn on-ice rivals, who meet as teenagers.

The first novel of Reid’s book series, Game Changers, which the novel Heated Rivalry hails from, centered on François Arnaud’s character Scott Hunter and Robbie G.K.’s character Kip Grady; it served as secondary material for the first season. The show’s season one cast was rounded out by Christina Chang, Dylan Walsh, Sophie Nélisse and Ksenia Daniela Kharlamova.

Season two of the series is filming in Toronto, and features a slew of new cast members. Williams and Storrie return to front the series, with Justice Smith, Charlie Gillespie, Daniel Diemer and Shaheen Jafargholi joining them in leading roles for the second season.

Tickets for Heated Rivalry‘s 4DX theatrical event are available at the box office and Regal’s website and mobile app.

#749. Scientists reverse liver cell aging and cut Alzheimer’s-linked protein in half

The liver may hold an unexpected key to fighting two of the most serious diseases associated with aging: Alzheimer's disease and heart disease. Scientists have discovered that restoring the function of aging liver cells can dramatically reduce harmful substances in the bloodstream, raising the possibility of treating diseases that affect organs far beyond the liver itself.

In a new study involving older rats, researchers at the Keck School of Medicine of USC found that an experimental drug called cinaciguat reversed important signs of aging in specialized liver cells. After just two weeks of treatment, levels of amyloid beta, a protein associated with Alzheimer's disease, dropped by half. Levels of LDL, commonly called bad cholesterol, also returned to those seen in younger animals.

The findings, published in the Journal of Biological Chemistry, also revealed a previously unknown way that liver cells communicate with one another. This discovery could help scientists develop treatments that restore the liver's ability to remove potentially harmful substances from the blood, possibly reducing the risk of Alzheimer's disease and atherosclerosis, a condition in which fatty deposits accumulate inside arteries.

Why the Liver Could Be Important for Alzheimer's

Although Alzheimer's primarily affects the brain, scientists are increasingly interested in how other organs might influence the disease. The liver plays a central role in filtering the blood and removing unwanted compounds, including substances that may contribute to disease when they accumulate.

The USC findings suggest that restoring this natural cleaning process could offer a different approach to preventing certain age-related illnesses. However, the results have so far been demonstrated only in rats, and additional studies are needed to establish whether the same benefits occur in humans.

"We need to do further translational work to see whether our findings might point to new therapies," said corresponding author Laurie DeLeve, MD, PhD, professor and vice chair for scientific affairs in the USC Department of Medicine. "We're hopeful, though, because the findings line up with a lot of epidemiological results showing age as a major risk factor for Alzheimer's and atherosclerosis, and liver damage as a risk factor for Alzheimer's."

Targeting the liver could be particularly valuable in Alzheimer's research, where efforts to develop treatments acting directly in the brain have faced an estimated 98% failure rate in clinical trials. One major obstacle is the blood-brain barrier, a protective system that limits which substances can enter the brain from the bloodstream. While this barrier helps shield the brain from harmful compounds, it also makes delivering certain medications extremely difficult.

"If we're right that the liver is impactful, what do we do about that?" said first author Sam de Leve, MA, a USC lab technician and child of Laurie DeLeve. "Rather than trying to get a drug through the blood-brain barrier, which is obnoxiously difficult, we could direct drugs to the liver, an organ where there might be more therapeutic impact and certainly an easier job of drug delivery."

Scientists Restore the Aging Liver's Natural Filters

To understand how liver aging affects the bloodstream, the researchers focused on a relatively understudied group of cells known as liver sinusoidal endothelial cells (LSECs).

These cells form the lining of tiny blood vessels inside the liver. Unlike most blood vessel walls, they contain numerous microscopic openings that function somewhat like the holes in a sieve. These openings allow larger molecules circulating in the blood to reach neighboring cells called hepatocytes, which carry out much of the liver's work processing and removing substances from the body.

As the liver ages, the openings in LSECs gradually become smaller or disappear. This makes it harder for certain large molecules to reach the cells responsible for clearing them, allowing more of these substances to remain in circulation.

One substance affected by this change is amyloid beta. This protein is especially important in Alzheimer's research because it can accumulate in the brain and form plaques, one of the disease's defining features.

Previous observations showed that the liver becomes less effective at removing amyloid beta as it ages. The researchers suspected that the gradual closing of the openings in LSECs might help explain why more of the protein remains in the bloodstream of older animals.

To investigate, they administered cinaciguat to aged rats for two weeks. They then compared the treated animals with two untreated groups, one consisting of older rats and the other of younger rats.

The results were striking. Cinaciguat restored the structure and function of the aging LSECs, reopening their microscopic pores and improving their ability to help clear substances from the blood. Amyloid beta concentrations fell by approximately 50%, reaching levels comparable to those in young rats. The untreated older animals showed no similar improvement.

The researchers also measured low-density lipoproteins (LDL), often referred to as "bad" cholesterol because elevated levels contribute to fatty deposits inside arteries. Over time, these deposits can restrict blood flow and increase the risk of heart disease.

Initially, LDL was included as a comparison measure rather than a substance expected to respond to treatment. Unlike larger molecules, LDL particles are small enough to leave the bloodstream without passing through the microscopic openings in LSECs. The scientists therefore expected cinaciguat to have little or no effect on LDL levels.

Instead, they discovered that LDL concentrations in treated older rats also fell to levels observed in young animals.

"We said, 'Wait, why did that go down? Clearly, there's more to this story,'" Sam de Leve said.

The unexpected finding suggested that the drug was doing more than simply reopening the liver's aging filters. It appeared to be restoring another important aspect of liver function.

Because previous research had shown that hepatocytes function better when LSECs are present, the team began examining how these two types of cells communicate.

Their investigation uncovered a previously unknown sequence of biochemical signals that helps coordinate the liver's ability to remove substances from the bloodstream.

A Hidden Communication Pathway Between Liver Cells

The researchers found that cinaciguat activates an enzyme called soluble guanylate cyclase inside LSECs. This triggers the cells to release a growth factor known as HB-EGF, which sends a signal to nearby hepatocytes.

In response, hepatocytes alter their surfaces in ways that allow them to capture more LDL and amyloid beta from the blood. This helps explain why the treatment reduced both substances, even though they do not rely on the same filtering mechanism.

Normally, aging interferes with the ability of LSECs to release HB-EGF. Cinaciguat restored this signaling process, allowing the liver cells to communicate more effectively and supporting the removal of substances that otherwise tend to accumulate with age.

The discovery identifies a potential new target for future drugs. Rather than focusing exclusively on the physical openings in LSECs, researchers may be able to develop therapies that restore the chemical signals responsible for helping the liver work efficiently.

Could Liver Rejuvenation Help Prevent Alzheimer's and Heart Disease?

According to the researchers, this is the first study to demonstrate that a drug can fully restore the structure and function of aging LSECs, including their ability to support the clearance of substances from the bloodstream.

It is also the first to show that a treatment directed at the liver can bring age-related elevations in circulating amyloid beta and LDL back to youthful levels.

These findings raise the possibility that cinaciguat, similar medications, or treatments targeting HB-EGF could eventually be used to counteract certain effects of liver aging. If those changes translate into meaningful protection against disease, they could provide new strategies for preventing Alzheimer's and cardiovascular problems.

For now, however, the findings represent an early step. Lowering amyloid beta in the bloodstream does not necessarily mean that amyloid plaques in the brain will decrease or that Alzheimer's disease can be prevented.

The researchers plan to continue studying cinaciguat in rats to determine whether its effects on amyloid beta actually translate into measurable protection against Alzheimer's disease.

They also hope the findings will encourage scientists studying other conditions, particularly atherosclerosis, to investigate how restoring liver function might influence disease development.

"We hope that people who are in fields like atherosclerosis research read this, and want to grab the idea for themselves," Sam de Leve said. "There are six different ways someone could go with this, and we can't do them all. So please, scoop us. We'd love it."

Additional researchers involved in the study include Xiangdong Wang, Helia Alavifard and Lily Dara, all affiliated with the Keck School of Medicine of USC.

The research received federal funding from the National Institutes of Health [R56AG071480, 5R01DK100580].

Mars Global Surveyor looked at the south pole of Mars and saw signs of possible climate change.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Nov. 7, 1996, NASA launched its Mars Global Surveyor mission. This was the first mission NASA sent to Mars in almost 20 years!

The Mars Global Surveyor spacecraft was an orbiter. It transmitted data from NASA's Mars rovers Sojourner, Spirit and Opportunity back to Earth. The spacecraft also did a lot of its own science. It found surface channels on Mars that appeared to have been created by running water.

Mars Global Surveyor looked at the south pole of Mars and saw signs of possible climate change. It also saw a mineral called hematite on Mars. Hematite usually forms in water. NASA then sent its Spirit and Opportunity rovers to look for the hematite, and both rovers found it near their landing sites.

Mars Global Surveyor survived much longer than expected. But a space maneuver accidentally exposed one of its batteries to the sun, and the spacecraft lost power. It fell silent forever in November 2006.

As the first successful Mars mission since the two Viking launches in 1975, Mars Global Surveyor ushered in a new era of exploration of the Red Planet, not only through its own contributions to orbit-based science, but by serving a relay for surface-based rovers. As such, it became a primary pipeline for multiple concurrent Mars missions."The [Mars Global Surveyor] mission overhauled scientists' understanding of Mars by studying the entire Martian surface, atmosphere and interior. Major findings included dramatic evidence that water still flows on Mars in short bursts down hillside gullies, and the identification of water-related mineral deposits leading to selection of a Mars rover landing site for a subsequent mission," read a NASA description of the probe.

Mars Global Surveyor sent back more than 240,000 images to Earth during its nine active years.Want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube.

#746. After Wasserman’s Exit, The Team Forms New Board of Directors

The 11-member board is comprised of leaders across the Mike Watts-led sports, music and representation giant as the rebranded firm charts its next chapter under Providence Equity Partners.

As it looks to chart a path away from its namesake founder, the Hollywood representation powerhouse The Team is installing a new board of directors stocked with leaders from key constituencies across the company.

The Westwood-based firm, formerly known as Wasserman, unveiled an 11-person board on Tuesday comprised of in-house exec members. Mike Watts, the CEO who took the helm amid founder Casey Wasserman’s tumultuous exit tied to an artist exodus in February, will serve on the board.

So too will Jon Liebman, the chief of Brillstein Entertainment Partners, the pioneering management and production firm that was acquired by Wasserman three years ago in a major expansion.

Kevin Shivers, who was promoted in April to co-president of music as part of the stabilization of that department (which had been bulked up through the acquisition of Paradigm’s roster five years ago), is also taking a seat on the board.

Leaders like Elizabeth Lindsey, who oversees the brands and properties business, Jason Ranne, who leads talent representation, the U.K.-based international chief Matthew Vandrau and CFO Elena Rochelli were also named to the board, as were C-suiters Davis Noell, Greg Brown and Scott Marimow.

Providence Equity Partners, the majority investor in The Team which formally bought out Wasserman’s interest after a bidding process over the summer, added its SVP Ahana Maken to the board and says that it will “name additional external board members in the coming months.” The firm has been invested in the company since 2022 when it took the place of prior backers RedBird Capital and Madrone Capital Partners.

The Team is one of the biggest players in the fast-growing sports representation space, along with CAA. And it has a large music roster that is being rebuilt after a slew of departures made waves in that space when Wasserman was linked to Ghislaine Maxwell over decades-old flirtatious emails unearthed by the Department of Justice in January.

The company, originally founded in 2002, has snapped up many multiple boutique agencies and had 4,000 employees as of earlier this year. Its latest acquisition was unveiled just last month, when it bought Outreach Talent Group, co-founded by Emilio Arciniega, which has its main base in London.

#745. Scientists say a forgotten particle may explain why the universe exists

Scientists have proposed a surprising new explanation for why the universe exists, and it centers on a mysterious particle that physicists have largely overlooked for decades. Their theory suggests this forgotten particle may have played a crucial role in shaping the early cosmos and allowing matter to survive after the Big Bang.

The research addresses one of the most fundamental mysteries in physics: why does the universe contain matter instead of nothing at all? Scientists believe matter and antimatter were produced in nearly equal amounts in the early universe. When these opposites encounter one another, they annihilate and release energy. If they had existed in perfectly equal quantities, virtually all matter could have disappeared, leaving no material to form stars, planets, or life.

Now, researchers from the University of Southampton and the Indian Institute of Technology Kanpur believe they may have found an important piece of the puzzle. Their explanation involves a little-understood relative of the neutrino, an extremely lightweight particle that rarely interacts with ordinary matter.

A Forgotten Particle With a Powerful Role in the Early Universe

The team focused on a type of particle known as a 'decoupled' heavy neutrino. Unlike ordinary neutrinos, this hypothetical heavier relative has generally been considered too weakly connected to other particles to significantly influence the universe.

However, the researchers found that its unusually long lifetime could have made it far more important than previously thought. According to their calculations, the particle may have survived long enough to temporarily dominate the universe's energy density as the cosmos cooled after the Big Bang.

That brief period of dominance could have altered how the early universe evolved, influencing the conditions that ultimately allowed matter to outnumber antimatter.

Dr. Rishav Roshan of the University of Southampton, an author of the study, explained:

"This decoupled heavy neutrino has long been dismissed as an irrelevant background detail in particle physics.

"However, it decays incredibly slowly. As the cosmos cooled after the Big Bang, the particle lived long enough that it temporarily took over the energy density of the universe and triggered a matter-dominated period."

The findings were published in Physical Review Letters, a scientific journal of the American Physical Society.

How a Heavy Neutrino Could Explain Why Matter Survived

Previous attempts to explain why matter prevailed over antimatter generally left out the decoupled heavy neutrino. Because it interacts so weakly with other particles, scientists assumed it would have little influence on the processes responsible for creating the imbalance.

The new research challenges that assumption. The team found that even a particle with extremely weak interactions could indirectly affect the conditions under which matter gained its crucial advantage.

This imbalance, known as matter and antimatter asymmetry, is essential to understanding our existence. For reasons physicists are still trying to explain, the early universe ended up with slightly more matter than antimatter. That small difference allowed some matter to remain after most particles and their antiparticles annihilated one another.

"The fact that we are here at all proves that an asymmetry between matter and antimatter occurred," added Dr. Roshan.

"The decoupled neutrino shifted the temperature in the early universe at which fundamental particles - like electrons and other leptons - interacted with their anti-particles with the help of Standard Model Higgs boson.

"This temperature acts like a switch that shapes how the matter-antimatter imbalance was built up."

The Higgs boson is a fundamental particle associated with the mechanism that gives many elementary particles their mass. In the researchers' proposed scenario, the heavy neutrino changed the temperature conditions governing important particle interactions involving the Higgs boson.

By shifting when these interactions occurred, the particle could have influenced how the imbalance between matter and antimatter developed. In other words, something long considered insignificant may have helped determine why the universe contains matter at all.

Ancient Gravitational Waves Could Reveal the Answer

The theory could also have important implications for understanding how the universe expanded in its earliest stages.

Study co-author Dr. Sudipta Show of the Indian Institute of Technology Kanpur said the findings suggest that the forgotten particle may have dramatically altered the expansion history of the young cosmos.

He added: "It offers us a new explanation for how matter won.

"The dramatic shift in the early expansion of the cosmos leaves distinct but detectable imprints of changes, for example on primordial gravitational waves.

"These gravitational wave signatures open up new avenues for us to unravel the evolution of the early universe after the Big Bang."

Gravitational waves are ripples in the fabric of space and time. Scientists believe processes in the extremely early universe may have generated primordial gravitational waves that carry information about conditions from that distant era.

According to the new theory, the temporary dominance of the heavy neutrino could have left recognizable signatures in those ancient signals. Detecting such patterns could eventually provide a way to investigate whether the proposed particle really influenced the universe's earliest evolution.

For now, the explanation remains theoretical. But it offers physicists a new possibility for solving one of cosmology's deepest mysteries: how matter survived when its encounter with antimatter could have left the universe almost entirely empty.

Materials provided by University of Southampton. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#743. NASA's Hubble and Webb discover ancient worlds that remember their past

NASA's Hubble and James Webb Space Telescopes have uncovered surprising clues about the earliest days of our solar system by examining some of the smallest and faintest objects ever observed beyond Neptune. The findings challenge expectations about how planets form and suggest that these distant, icy bodies have preserved evidence of their origins for billions of years.

For the first time, astronomers combined observations from Hubble and Webb to investigate trans-Neptunian objects (TNOs), tiny bodies that travel around the Sun far beyond Neptune's orbit. Researchers discovered 27 previously unknown objects, but their findings revealed an unexpected puzzle. There were fewer small objects than some theories predicted, and their colors closely resembled those of much larger objects in the same distant regions.

These frozen remnants offer a rare opportunity to study the materials that eventually became planets. Most are extraordinarily difficult to detect, shining more than 100 million times more faintly than objects visible to the naked eye. Two related studies published in The Astronomical Journal examined the newly identified objects to learn more about their sizes, compositions, and ancient history.

Ancient Building Blocks of the Solar System

Scientists believe planets began forming when tiny particles of dust and pebbles orbiting the young Sun gradually accumulated into larger bodies. Over time, these materials formed objects roughly the size of cities, known as "planetesimals." These early building blocks eventually combined to create the planets we see today.

However, that final stage of growth did not occur for many objects beyond Neptune. Instead of developing into full-sized planets, countless smaller bodies remained, preserving evidence of the solar system's earliest period of formation.

To investigate these distant survivors, research teams led by PhD candidates at the University of Victoria in Canada, working under the guidance of the National Research Council of Canada, and Northern Arizona University in Flagstaff conducted the deepest survey of trans-Neptunian objects to date. Both space telescopes observed the same region of sky simultaneously, with Hubble collecting visible light and Webb capturing infrared light.

By combining these observations, astronomers could examine the objects' colors, estimate their sizes, and determine how they orbit the Sun. Their colors are especially valuable because they provide clues about the chemical makeup of their surfaces, much like fingerprints that reveal an object's identity and history.

The researchers focused on two distinct populations of trans-Neptunian objects, known as dynamically "cold" and dynamically "hot" TNOs. These descriptions refer to their orbital behavior rather than their temperatures.

Cold objects have largely remained in the regions where they originally formed. They follow relatively circular paths around the Sun and stay close to the plane in which most of the solar system's planets orbit.

Hot objects have experienced a much more turbulent history. They originally formed between the present-day orbits of Uranus and Neptune but were scattered outward as the giant planets shifted positions early in the solar system's development. Their current orbits are much more elongated, and they travel above and below the solar system's main orbital plane.

Despite these dramatically different histories, the two populations revealed an unexpected similarity. Even the smallest objects appear to have retained surface characteristics resembling those of their larger counterparts.

Tiny Worlds Preserve Their Ancient Origins

Before the observations, scientists suspected that smaller TNOs would show clear evidence of repeated collisions over billions of years. Impacts could have fractured the objects and exposed fresh material, potentially changing their surface compositions and colors.

Instead, the newly discovered objects displayed the same general color relationships seen among larger TNOs. This suggests that collisions may have altered their surfaces much less than expected.

One possibility is that these objects have experienced fewer impacts than astronomers previously assumed. Another is that their surfaces somehow retain their original compositions even after collisions. Researchers have not yet determined which explanation is correct.

"You could imagine a scenario where getting knocked around and fragmented would change the surface composition, and then you would see a different surface color for tiny TNOs compared to their larger siblings. So it's really fascinating to see that the smallest objects are somehow 'remembering' and preserving the history of how they were made," said Northern Arizona University PhD candidate Anastasia Morgan, who led the study of color and composition.

"These dynamically 'hot' TNOs retain a signature of where they were born, even though they've been orbitally scrambled since then," said co-author David Trilling of Northern Arizona University.

The observations indicate that both hot and cold TNOs have maintained color patterns linked to their formation, with surprisingly little apparent change since the solar system's beginnings. These ancient objects may therefore preserve important information about the environments in which they first took shape.

Webb Finds Fewer Tiny Worlds Than Expected

The James Webb Space Telescope also provided another important piece of the puzzle. Its observations allowed scientists to examine how many objects exist at different sizes, revealing an unexpected resemblance between the two populations.

Although hot and cold TNOs formed in different parts of the early solar system, their overall size distributions were remarkably alike. This suggests that the processes responsible for creating planetesimals may have operated in much the same way across different environments.

"It's very interesting that the process of planetesimal formation ends up producing the same distribution of sizes for both cold and hot populations, despite forming in different regions of the early solar system. The process seems to be insensitive to disk conditions, producing similar planetesimal sizes whether the disk is hot or cold, and dense or fluffy," said University of Victoria PhD candidate Marielle Eduardo, who led the study on size distribution.

The researchers also identified a surprising shortage of very small TNOs compared with predictions from some existing planet formation models. Understanding why fewer objects were detected could help scientists refine their explanations of how the solar system's original building blocks developed.

Webb's extraordinary sensitivity made it possible to discover 27 exceptionally faint objects. One was so dim that detecting it would be comparable to standing on Earth and spotting a small swarm of fireflies on the Moon.

The smallest object measured just 3 miles (5 kilometers) across, making it approximately five times smaller than the objects detectable with even the most sensitive telescopes on the ground.

Hubble and Webb Reveal New Clues to Planet Formation

These discoveries depended on the complementary capabilities of NASA's two powerful space observatories. Hubble's ability to detect visible light and Webb's sensitivity to infrared light gave scientists a more complete picture of the distant objects than either telescope could have provided independently.

Together, the telescopes have opened a new window into a largely unexplored population of ancient solar system remnants. Their surprising similarities, preserved surface characteristics, and unexpected numbers offer important clues about the processes that shaped the planets billions of years ago.

#742. ‘Nobody Wants This’ Star Timothy Simons Reveals Biggest Season 3 Concern and Looks to Season 4: “They Burned One Another — So They’re Even”

The 'Veep' actor also opens up about his co-stars and creator weighing in on Adam Brody's Gaza comments, and how being on the Jewish show has shaped his own views on religion.

[This story contains spoilers from Nobody Wants This season two.]

When Timothy Simons and Justine Lupe found out that this would be such a big season for their Nobody Wants This duo Sasha and Morgan, respectively, Simons said he and his co-star had some key concerns.

“We are very limb-forward people. We have a lot of arms,” he tells The Hollywood Reporter with a laugh. “Even weeks before we left [to film the] New York [episode], I said to our director, ‘Hey, can we talk about the blocking for this? Because we just don’t want to look like muppets.'” Related Stories Movies 'Steps' Review: A Stellar Voice Cast Including Amanda Seyfried, Ali Wong and Bette Midler Gets Stuck in a Tortured Revisionist Fairy Tale TV 'Nobody Wants This' Stars Hint at Season 4 and Declare Timothy Simons "the Lead of the Show Now"

When it came time to film the seventh episode of season two, “Watch What Happens,” Simons said he and Lupe took the trust and responsibility of their story getting such a spotlight seriously. The result was a bottle episode that is getting rave reviews for taking Sasha and Morgan out of Los Angeles and landing them in a bed together, only to blow up their romance shortly after when Esther (Jackie Tohn), Sasha’s estranged wife, reveals she and Sasha also slept together. The finale leaves the trio, once again, in a love triangle. But it’s slightly different this time around.

“It’s a pretty mature choice for Sasha to be like, ‘This might be the right thing, but it’s the wrong time.’ I also think there was a fair amount of maturity in what Morgan did after years and years of not trying and running from things. So I don’t know which way it’s going to go,” he says of how season three ends, now that the hit Netflix series has been officially renewed for season four.

Below, the Veep actor shares his hopes for next season (the writers room has been up and running), and weighs in on co-star Adam Brody’s Gaza comments, how the show has shaped his views on religion and why Nobody Wants This is not likely to bring such conversations to the Roklov dinner table. “Adam and Erin are both immensely passionate about the views they’ve spoken to. I know they have spoken personally about it before. It’s always respectful,” he says.

So whose idea was it to dye your hair blonde for the season?

I had done it for fun for the Emmys a couple of years ago, when we were there with the show after the first season. All the writers saw it sort of separately and each individually had the idea to write that in. Then they all got together and realized they all had that same thought, so they wrote it in and I had to keep it.

Were you over being a blonde by the end of filming?

I actually loved it and thought it fit the vibe, because Sasha is going through something. Although I wasn’t going through something, I could definitely see how it would fit someone like Sasha going through something. And I will say, if you have hair as short and dark as mine, it requires more upkeep than you think and is a bit of a continuity nightmare. I didn’t get sick of it through the entire season; I really did like it. But after, I did get sick of the upkeep so I’m back to brunette. I’m rocking my real self now and it feels good.

When did you find out this was going to be such a big season for Sasha and Morgan (Justine Lupe)? Can you take me inside that conversation with your creator/showrunners when they first laid it out for you?

Justine and I went into the writers room. They had outlined the entire season and pitched it out to Netflix, and Netflix OK’d it. We do that every year — we sit down and they bring us through the broad strokes. We talk about it a lot and throw out ideas that they can either take or leave. So it was in the writers room early on when we found out.

We’re a 10-episode show and they told us that episode seven was going to be dedicated to just the two of us. As a performer, that feels incredible that they have that amount of trust in Justine and I to hand over responsibility of a full episode just to us. That is immensely flattering. I think we both had the same reaction. We took that seriously. We took that trust and responsibility seriously.

That episode is getting raves for being like a mini rom-com bottle episode. You and Justine are close friends. What was it like to play out Sasha and Morgan’s sexual tension, and eventually sleep together?

We’ve always had similar styles, or at least similar thought processes on performance, which I think is why we get along so well and have chemistry. We have a lot of mutual friends. There was a lot of trust in Justine, at least on my side, from very early on.

We are very limb-forward people. We’re very lanky. We have a lot of arms. (Laughs.) And we just didn’t want to look like muppets when we ended up kissing. So we talked a lot to our director, Richard Shepard, who is incredible. Even weeks before we left for New York I was like, “Hey, can we talk about the blocking for this? Because we just don’t want to look like muppets.”

Because the moment they kiss, if that moment doesn’t work, then none of it works. You built it all up to that. And if we look like muppets, it would undercut the whole thing. But it’s our jobs and we’re close, and we joked around about it a lot. But both of us are professionals about it.

Did you see the twist coming of Sasha and Esther (Jackie Tohn) reuniting?

I didn’t. I feel like hooking up with your ex is a thing that has happened to a lot of people. You can’t just all of a sudden shake off a 20-year relationship and not have that come up again. I didn’t necessarily see it coming, but that felt like something that does naturally happen sometimes. So it did take me by surprise a little bit. But in a good way. Conflict and confrontations are good for drama!

The finale ends unresolved about who he is going to pick, if anyone. Where would you say his heart lies by the end of the season?

I’ve mentioned this to Justine before. Justine is such an incredible performer and can access such an immense vulnerability — especially in that scene in the parking garage. There were times as an actor that I was like, “Can we just fix this for her so she doesn’t have to feel like this?!” But there was a fair amount of maturity that I didn’t even realize until I watched the season. It’s a pretty mature choice for him to be like, “This might be the right thing, but it’s the wrong time.” I don’t think he’s ever said that before. He very much went along with whatever anyone else wanted for him, and so I do think it was a mature choice for him to make to be like, “It seems like not the right thing in either direction.”

So I don’t know which way it’s going to go. But it does seem like he is a little bit like, “I have to back off of both of these things for a little bit.”

Do you think Morgan could be mature enough to get over being burned by Sasha, if he does want to pursue a relationship with her?

I also think there was a fair amount of maturity in what Morgan did after years and years of not trying and running from things. And being willing to take a risk that she’s never taken before and not half-assing anything. I feel like if she is taking steps in that direction, and there could be a world. Also, I would throw in that they kind of burned one another. She kind of burned him when she ran away and he kind of burned her when she said no. So they are still at an even point.

We heard the writers room has been up. Erin Foster was recently said on Dax Shepard’s podcast that they were writing a role for him. Have any ideas been shared with you yet? [Note: This interview occurred before the official season four renewal.]

I would absolutely love to do more of it. I’ve enjoyed the cast and crew and writers and directors of this show immensely. So doing more of it? I’m 100 percent in favor for. But I’m not being cagey when I tell you that I don’t have any idea what they’re talking about, because I haven’t gone in to do the sit down yet.

What decisions would you like to see Sasha making in season four?

The writers are always coming up with better things than me. I have my personal feelings, but they will always come up with better ideas. Either way, he and Esther reconciling… clearly, they do love one another. They built a life together, so you’d like to see them work through that. Maybe they slip back into old habits and all that work he did to put himself together a little bit more goes by the wayside.

And I love the idea of two weirdos like Sasha and Morgan finding each other and that working out, but maybe that’s too messy with the family. There are pros and cons on either side, so I’m interested to see what the writers come up with.

This season got a lot of attention for two things. First, because of the big endings for both Noah (Adam Brody) and Joanne (Kristen Bell), and you and Morgan. But also because of your creator Erin Foster and co-stars responding to Brody’s Gaza comments. Do you feel like there is a responsibility for your writers and cast to speak out because the show is a Jewish show? How do you feel about it, and how do you feel about being asked about it?

Adam and Erin are both immensely passionate about the views they’ve spoken to. And I do think the way Erin said it… they work together really well. I know they have spoken personally about it before. It’s always respectful, and that’s one of the great things about Adam is that he is kind and thoughtful and empathetic and will talk to anybody, even if their views don’t align with his, to try to fight for a safer world for everybody. That’s what’s underneath all of it.

Erin said the show is a love letter to Judaism. After playing a Jewish character on this show, how has that shaped or informed your views on Judaism?

I’ve never been a religious person. I didn’t grow up religious. I had an Irish-Catholic grandmother, but religion was not a huge part of my family or my life coming into the show. But I will say, my dad passed away recently…

Thank you. There was a moment when I got back to Los Angeles after the [funeral] service; we have neighbors who we’ve been good friends with since our kids were in kindergarten together, and they invited me to go to Shabbat at the temple they go to in our neighborhood. There’s a mourner’s circle [the Kaddish] and it was incredible to go to a temple and be welcomed in and be able to say my dad’s name out loud and a rabbi told me, “May his memory be a blessing.”

Even as a non-religious person — I’m certainly not a scholar — there are a lot of rituals surrounding death and mourning and grief that I have learned through this experience of learning more about Judaism that even if I am not religious, have given me a lot of comfort.

Shortly after my dad died, my college roommate died of brain cancer, so I’m in a mourner’s circle saying two names. You realize why religion has been around so long as a guide through moments of grief and to try to find some sense of comfort. That is something that, albeit, I did now know coming in[to this show]. There has been a lot of stuff I learned that has helped me in my day-to-day life because of this experience.

I’m really sorry about your friend and about your dad.

Thank you, I appreciate it. It’s been a little bit of a rough summer, but we’re working through it.

Nobody Wants This isn’t a political show. It’s a feel-good show. Have you had conversations with the writers about if the show would get more current as it goes, or is that not the ethos of the show? Will the extended Roklov family ever be arguing over the war at the dinner table?

Yeah, that has not been the language of this show so far, and I would also throw back to you that the writers always know better than me. If they want to find a way into that, [they will]. Just like I said before about a love triangle, they are going to know how to best attack it.

Your kids [14-year-old twins] love Nobody Wants This. When will you show them Veep?

I actually, for a very long time, had not appeared in a single project that they could have watched. (Laughs.) Now we are at a point where with some outliers, we can pretty much show them everything. We have a lot of movie nights as a family where we’ll show them Rear Window and Mad Max: Fury Road and John Wick. So I do think they are ready to watch Veep. However, there has to be a conversation about, “This is not language that you use in school or with teachers, or in any sort of important situation.”

Would you want to do a Veep revival, or is the real world still getting in the way of that?

Would I love to be in the room with all of those people again? The answer is 100 percent, yes. But we also live in a world that is un-satirizable. The show would be completely different and honestly, what are we going to do that’s dumber than what’s happening? We live in a world that’s beyond parody, so how could we possibly parody it? Would I love to work with those people again? That would be amazing. But I don’t know how it would fit.

I’m glad the show has stayed relevant and people still enjoy it and still see a reflection of the world now, even though we made it so long ago. It’s been six or seven years since it went off the air. That’s amazing. I would sacrifice a little bit of the longtail of the show if the world were a little bit less chaotic. I would really like for fewer people to tell me Veep was still relevant if the world was a little better.

Nobody Wants This season two is now streaming all episodes on Netflix.
